items.title: Michal: Opposition is panicking, 'catastrophe narratives' are not true
items.summary: Prime Minister and Reform Party chairman Kristen Michal said calls by the opposition to hold early elections show the parties are "panicking" because the "catastrophe narratives" about the poor economic situation they have relied on are no longer true.
items.body_text:
Michal: Opposition is panicking, 'catastrophe narratives' are not true
Prime Minister and Reform Party chairman Kristen Michal said calls by the opposition to hold early elections show the parties are "panicking" because the "catastrophe narratives" about the poor economic situation they have relied on are no longer true.
On Saturday, the most popular opposition party, Isamaa, published a statement calling for a vote of no confidence in the Reform-Eesti 200 minority government and new elections. Similar comments were made by EKRE and Center earlier this week.
The next Riigikogu elections will take place in March 2027.
Michal wrote on social media in response: "The opposition's narrative of a poor economy no longer holds up. They are in a hurry because this talk that we are in an economic quagmire will not last until the elections. This story is built on lies and propaganda, which by now have also been publicly refuted with facts by Statistics Estonia."
The Reform chairman stressed that during his years as prime minister, the economy has grown continuously and wage growth has been considerably faster than price growth.
Michal said that the opposition's negative narrative about the energy sector is also not true.
"In June and July this year, Finland had the cheapest electricity exchange price in the European Union, and Estonia had the second-cheapest after Finland. The price increases that plagued Estonia because of the shock of the war and trends in the global economy are declining. In July, our price growth was the lowest in the European Union," he wrote.
Michal also claimed that the opposition lost the initiative in the presidential election, which will be held next week: "EKRE is not participating, Isamaa is unable to remain united and the Center Party wants, unconstitutionally, to prohibit MPs from electing the president."
He said that the opposition's nervousness does not stem from the country doing badly, because Estonia has done considerably better over the past two years than previously thought.
"The entire joint strategy of EKRE, Isamaa and the Center Party is built on the idea that the Estonian state and its people are doing badly. When the economy does better and confidence among businesses and people improves, the opposition has a problem because its political fuel runs out. When the economy was thought to be contracting, the opposition blamed the government for the contraction. The economy and consumer confidence are growing. Our plan has borne fruit, the decisions, reforms and budget choices are right. The growth is connected to this," Michal said.
"People, life and facts have put an end to the catastrophe narratives, and that is why the opposition is panicking. Economic growth needs to be given momentum; that should be the goal of all parties. EKREIKE's political gamesmanship is not in the interests of Estonia's economic growth or its people," the prime minister concluded, using the acronym for the previous EKRE-Isamaa-Center coalition (2019-2021).
--

items.title: Security guards report more cases of young people taking drugs
items.summary: Security guards are increasingly concerned about young people using drugs in public places. The police and the National Institute for Health Development said that social media has made drugs more accessible.
items.body_text:
Security guards report more cases of young people taking drugs
Security guards are increasingly concerned about young people using drugs in public places. The police and the National Institute for Health Development said that social media has made drugs more accessible.
Security company Viking Security has seen an increasing number of cases this year in which minors openly sell or use not only cannabis but also harder drugs in shopping centers and entertainment venues.
"Drug use among young people is very noticeable because it affects them much more strongly than alcohol and their pattern of behaviour changes," explained Sander Nurgamaa, head of the security company's video surveillance centre.
"At one centre in Tartu, a group of young people went into the toilet and when they came out, one of them collapsed. During a subsequent check, a small bag containing traces of white powder was found inside a snus container in their possession."
Studies by the National Institute for Health Development (TAI) show that 30 percent of minors have used drugs at some point in their lives, which is a worryingly high figure.
Head of the narcotics department Katri Abel-Ollo said there are very few young people who do not consume alcohol but do use drugs.
"Often it is not a choice between one or the other. We are not actually seeing a huge increase with alcohol and tobacco either. It is still a third who experiment with and use such substances," she explained, adding, however, that the number of users has fallen over the past 12 months.
However, the Police confirmed that alcohol remains considerably more widespread than drugs.
"Young people intoxicated by alcohol are certainly caught in much greater numbers than those intoxicated by drugs. Smoking or vaping is certainly a problem, and there is also property crime and crime against persons, but our call-outs do not indicate that there has been a significant increase in drug use," said Rait Pikaro, head of the criminal bureau at the Police and Border Guard Board's Northern Prefecture.
The security company, police and TAI all said that drugs have become very easily accessible. While alcohol can be bought from a shop, criminals sell drugs online.
"There is often no longer even any person-to-person contact. Substances are handed over through hiding places and payment is made in cryptocurrency. In that sense, criminals have clearly used social media instant messaging apps to their advantage. And this certainly poses a greater threat to young people than the street dealer of the past," Pikaro added.
--

items.title: IRMCT judge begins investigation into circumstances of Ratko Mladic’s death
items.summary: International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT) Judge Iain Bonomy has arrived in The Hague and begun an investigation into the circums
items.body_text:
IRMCT judge begins investigation into circumstances of Ratko Mladicâs death
International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (IRMCT) Judge Iain Bonomy has arrived in The Hague and begun an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, the Mechanism said Sunday.
Oglas
Bonomy visited the United Nations Detention Unit and the prison hospital where Mladic had been receiving treatment on Saturday, according to the IRMCT.
The investigation remains ongoing, while details are being kept confidential at this stage.
The Mechanism said it remained in regular contact with Mladicâs family, including regarding arrangements for the transfer of his remains.
Dutch authorities confirmed on Saturday that they would not open a criminal investigation into Mladicâs death and that no autopsy would be conducted.
Mladic, the former commander of the Army of Republika Srpska (VRS), died on August 27 in a detention hospital in Scheveningen while serving a life sentence.
He had been in the custody of the UN tribunal system since his arrest in Serbia in 2011, following nearly 16 years on the run.
The former Bosnian Serb military commander was sentenced to life imprisonment after being convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war committed during the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Mladic was convicted of genocide for the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed.
He was also convicted over the campaign of sniping and shelling against civilians during the siege of Sarajevo, persecution and other crimes committed across Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the taking of UN personnel hostage.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) convicted Mladic in 2017. His life sentence was upheld on appeal by the IRMCT in 2021.

items.title: Gervalla: Kosovo will not sacrifice rule of law to appease EU
items.summary: Kosovo’s acting Justice Minister Donika Gervalla has rejected European Union criticism of a decision concerning Kosovo Serb judges who resigned in 202
items.body_text:
Gervalla: Kosovo will not sacrifice rule of law to appease EU
Kosovoâs acting Justice Minister Donika Gervalla has rejected European Union criticism of a decision concerning Kosovo Serb judges who resigned in 2022, saying Kosovo would not sacrifice the rule of law for what she described as an EU âpolicy of appeasementâ.
Gervalla was responding to an EU statement expressing deep regret over the Kosovo Judicial Councilâs (KJC) decision to accept the resignations of Kosovo Serb judges even though they had withdrawn them.
The EU said the decision appeared incompatible with Kosovo law, due process and overall rule of law requirements and called for conditions to be created for the reintegration of Kosovo Serb judicial personnel.
Brussels also stressed that Kosovo is constitutionally a multi-ethnic society and that its justice system must reflect its ethnic diversity.
In a Facebook post, Gervalla said she could not remain silent over what she described as attempts to challenge the implementation of Kosovo law by independent institutions or impose political interpretations and preferences on them.
She argued that the KJC decision was fully in line with Kosovoâs Constitution and legislation.
âThe Law on the Kosovo Judicial Council, in Article 26, explicitly establishes the Councilâs obligation, in the event of the resignation of a judge or prosecutor, to submit a proposal for dismissal from office to the president,â Gervalla wrote.
âThese resignations were submitted in 2022. Almost four years have passed. The judges in question have not performed their duties for approximately four years.â
âTell us which law was violatedâ
Gervalla challenged those who claim the decision was contrary to Kosovo law to identify the specific legal provision that had been violated.
âTell us which law was violated. Which article? Which provision?â she said.
She asked which Kosovo law allows someone to resign from a position in the judiciary, not perform that role for almost four years and then return to the same position.
Gervalla said it was unacceptable for a Judicial Council decision based, in her view, on Kosovoâs constitutional and legal framework to be questioned for political reasons.
âIt is not possible to demand that Kosovo implement the law while at the same time putting pressure on its institutions when they implement it,â she wrote.
She said Kosovoâs European partners should support the country when its institutions make decisions based on law, ânot only when the results are politically convenientâ.
Gervalla acknowledged that representation of different communities within the judiciary is a constitutional obligation, but said this could not be used to relativise the law or judicial independence.
âThe Republic of Kosovo cannot sacrifice its rule of law for the sake of an EU policy of appeasement, to the detriment of the constitutional and legal order of the Republic of Kosovo,â Gervalla said.
âIn the Republic of Kosovo, no one is above the law. Absolutely no one. No individual. No institution. And no political pressure, local or international.â

items.title: Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
items.summary: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said the UN war crimes tribunal in The Hague was guilty of "uncivilised" and "unjustifiable" behaviour for not releasing the Bosnian Serb genocide convict before his death this week.
items.body_text:
Serbian President Vucic Says UN Court ‘Wanted Mladic to Die Behind Bars’
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said on Friday that “The Hague wanted [Ratko] Mladic to die behind bars, not in a hospital” because the UN court declined to release the former Bosnian Serb military chief for palliative care in Belgrade ahead of his death.
“We have seen that they did not want to allow the general to die in Serbia, where he wanted to die. That is uncivilised behaviour, behaviour without precedent and without justification,” Vucic said in his first public statement after the death of Mladic on Thursday.
He added that he had been in close contact with Mladic’s family, and that Serbia would ensure that the former Bosnian Serb military leader’s funeral would be “done in a dignified and proper manner”.
On Thursday, Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic said that Mladic would be buried with state honours in Serbia. Vucic introduced a note of doubt, however, saying that everything published in the press had been inaccurate.
Vucic also claimed that “the West” had only found Serbs guilty of war crimes from the 1990s.
“Do I believe in justice from The Hague? I never have, and I still do not,” he said.
“All those who took part in crimes against Serbs in the former Yugoslavia were always either acquitted or given token sentences, only for those decisions to later be changed on appeal and the defendants ultimately released,” he added.
Vucic’s statement, slamming the Hague court, echoes Thursday’s reactions to Mladic’s death in pro-government media, among members of the governing Serbian Progressive Party, from hardline nationalist politicians Vojislav Seselj and Aleksandar Vulin and from Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik.
Serbia is an EU candidate state, and on Friday, the European Commission told Radio Free Europe that it was up to the Belgrade authorities to decide what role they would play in the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.
However, the Commission warned: “The European Commission considers any glorification of war criminals to be contrary to the most fundamental European values and to have no place either in the EU or in countries that are candidates for EU membership.”

items.title: Montenegro President Summons Security Council Over ‘Destabilisation Threats’
items.summary: President Jakov Milatovic has called an emergency session of the country’s Defence and Security Council after claims that two neighbour states are seeking to destabilise Montenegro and obstruct its EU accession progress.
items.body_text:
Montenegro President Summons Security Council Over ‘Destabilisation Threats’
President Jakov Milatovic’s office said on Friday that he has called the heads of the country’s security sector Defence and Security Council after allegations by Prime Minister Milojko Spajic that the country faces “hybrid threats” from two of its neighbours.
Spajic claimed that officials from at least two countries in the region are involved in coordinated activity aimed at destabilising Montenegro and undermining its path towards European Union membership.
Milatovic’s office said the security chiefs will be asked to provide precise information on Spajic’s allegations, as well as a comprehensive assessment of the country’s security situation.
Spajic said on Thursday that Montenegro had “serious operational security information” that threats would accompany the country’s expected progress in opening new EU negotiating chapters. Montenegro is currently seen as the frontrunner among Balkan states to become the next EU member.
“According to our information, such activities are aimed at destabilising Montenegro, with the expected support of certain political actors and part of the media scene in our country,” Spajic posted on X.
On Friday, Montenegrin newspaper Vijesti reported that Serbia and Albania are the two countries referred to by Spajic.
Vijesti quoted an unnamed source who said that some key players in the region were unhappy with Montenegro’s rapid progress toward European integration and wanted to slow it down.
Another anonymous source quoted by the newspaper claimed that a senior government official was vulnerable because of compromising information that could be used by foreign powers. The source suggested that the official’s political party might leave the ruling coalition as a result.
Milatovic’s office said that the president was concerned by the reports, and that “the public has the right to know which official this is”. But it added that serious security issues should not be used to score political points.
“Issues concerning the security and stability of the state must be addressed responsibly, based on facts and through the institutions of the system,” it said.
The warning did not stop some prominent figures connecting the security issue to responses to the death on Thursday of the Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic.
After parliamentary speaker Andrija Mandic stated that he had sent condolences to the former general’s family, the head of Montenegro’s Islamic Community, Rifat Fejzic, asked if politicians who “mourn war criminals [are] in collusion with this hybrid war?”
Albania’s Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Ferit Hoxha has rejected the suggestion that his country was part of any “destabilising scenario” in Montenegro. Posting on X, Hoxha insisted that the allegations could not “artificially create problems between our two countries”.
“Although no formal accusations have been articulated against Albania, I wish to state clearly and strongly that Albania is not, and cannot be, part of any destabilising scenario, whether in Montenegro – a neighbour, friend, partner, and NATO ally with whom we share the same EU membership goal – or anywhere else,” he wrote.

items.title: Week in Review: Hopes and Dilemmas
items.summary: From Turkey’s search for peace to Serbia’s creeping elections, our selection of Premium stories takes a look at the hopes and dilemmas bubbling away in the background of these developments.
items.body_text:
Week in Review: Hopes and Dilemmas
Forcing a deal
The question of who owns Bosnia and Herzegovina’s state property is a major point of dispute and an unresolved issue on the country’s path away from supervision by the Office of the High Representative and towards membership of the EU. Not surprising, perhaps, in a country where the core issue of sovereignty is contested.
Intractable though the issue may seem, might there be movement towards resolving it? Washington’s newly-discovered interest in energy, mining and infrastructure projects in the country is putting the spotlight on this issue. Now the question is whether Bosnia will solve the issue of state property on Washington’s terms or its own.
Read more: Could Trump’s Administration Force a Deal on Bosnia’s State Property? (August 21, 2026)
Pre-campaigning
Will he? Won’t he? For much of the year, Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic has kept the public guessing over if and when he might call early elections. Indeed, Vucic himself may still not have made up his mind.
But in the meantime, the Serbian leader has been on a blitz tour of the country, visiting factories, checking on roadworks and hearing the pleas and grievances of ordinary people. The pace and scale of the campaign have caught many by surprise. In his opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Bojan Vranic dissects the motivation for Vucic’s manoeuvres.
Read more: Hanging Out: Serbia’s Ruling Party Funfair is About Suppressing Voter Turnout (August 24, 2026)
Courting Trump
As the conflict between the US and Iran limps on, ordinary Americans are feeling the pinch. So, it seems, are Donald Trump’s approval ratings on handling the economy, as November’s crucial mid-term elections approach.
Yet while Trump’s appeal may be tanking in the US, his star still shines in faraway corners of the world, including the Balkans. In her regular ‘Letter from Washington’ column, Jovana Djurovic takes a look at the latest attempts by Balkan countries and their leaders to ingratiate themselves with Trump.
Read more: Letter from Washington: Buying Trump’s Favour with UFC in Serbia, Arms in Albania (August 27, 2026)
Making peace
As Turkey moves to end its four decade-long conflict with the Kurdish PKK militant group, the prospect of peace is opening up new dilemmas for Kurdish villagers displaced by years of fighting. Tens of thousands of people have fled areas of fighting over the decades, leaving several thousand villages depopulated.
With peace apparently within grasp, some of those displaced are revisiting their homes and villages. While many long to return for good, rebuilding normal life in most of these villages will be anything but simple, as our report shows.
Read more: As Turkey Makes Peace, Kurdish Villagers Who Fled Conflict Contemplate Return (August 25, 2026)
Brewing resistance
Have people across the Balkans had enough of foreign-backed luxury development projects? Campaigns against two very prominent projects linked to the Trump family in Serbia and Albania seem to suggest so.
In his opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Ted Todorovic-Thomas takes a look at whether something is stirring across the region. He argues that the trend has deeper and more long-standing roots.
Read more: Across the Balkans, Foreign-Backed Luxury Developments Cause Local Anger (August 25, 2026)
Missing millions
In 2017, a private company agreed a concession with the Albanian government to build and operate a waste disposal and incineration facility outside the capital, Tirana. By 2023, some 104 million euros had been transferred to the company in public funds and other revenues.
But there was a catch. When the state took over the project in 2023, there was next to nothing to show for all the money spent. Our investigation takes a look at the ongoing trial over the missing money behind Albania’s ghost incinerators.
Read more: Waste Money Wasted: The Millions of Euros Behind Albania’s Ghost Incinerators (August 21, 2026)

items.title: New Miniature Sculpture Recalls a Forgotten Chapter in Budapest’s History
items.summary: Another miniature sculpture by Mihály Kolodko has appeared in Budapest, this time commemorating a little-known chapter of the city’s history at the Buda end of Liberty Bridge: seaplanes once carried passengers from the banks of the Danube to Lake Balaton and Vienna. The miniature sculpture, titled “The Last Flight,” was placed on one of the […] The post New Miniature Sculpture Recalls a Forgotten Chapter in Budapest’s History appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
Mihály Kolodko’s latest sculpture depicts a Khanty hunter with a fallen deer near the Rákóczi Bridge. Continue reading
Another miniature sculpture by Mihály Kolodko has appeared in Budapest, this time commemorating a little-known chapter of the city’s history at the Buda end of Liberty Bridge: seaplanes once carried passengers from the banks of the Danube to Lake Balaton and Vienna.
The miniature sculpture, titled “The Last Flight,” was placed on one of the rocks beside the Buda side of Liberty Bridge.
The location is no coincidence:
Between 1923 and 1926, the site was home to the seaplane port of Aeroexpress.
The seaplanes of the era departed from here for Lake Balaton and Vienna.
Aeroexpress was an airline founded in 1923 by Count Endre Jankovich-Besán and Junkers Flugzeug AG of Dessau.
In 1923, the company received permission to operate three routes:
- Budapest–Székesfehérvár–Nagykanizsa–Zagreb,
- Budapest–Prague, and
- Budapest–Bucharest.
Its fleet consisted of six Junkers F 13 passenger aircraft.
The company began operating charter flights in June 1923, initially only within Hungary. Later, flights between Vienna and Budapest were launched in cooperation with ÖLAG (Österreichische Luftverkehrs). By 1925, these flights operated several times a day.
The company’s most famous pilot was ocean aviator György Endresz.
A Banat Swabian by birth, he became famous for his “Justice for Hungary” flight in 1931, which made a spectacular statement against the Treaty of Trianon.
The Budapest seaplane port of Aeroexpress was located in front of the Gellért Hotel, while in Vienna it was situated at the Reichsbrücke over the Danube. Apart from Austria, the company was unable to conclude air transport agreements with other countries. Its domestic and international flights proved unprofitable, and it ceased operations on January 1, 1930. In 1936, the company was removed from the register of airlines.
Today, a memorial plaque at the Buda end of Liberty Bridge commemorates the former port. Mihály Kolodko’s new sculpture commemorates this forgotten chapter of Budapest’s history, marking the 100th anniversary of the port’s closure.
Via turizmus.com, Featured image: Fortepan / Weygand Tibor

items.body_text:
The event will offer a wider range of programs than a regular day at the zoo.Continue reading
The red deer rut is already in full swing, with the stags bellowing in Gemenc (southern Hungary), one of Europe’s largest contiguous floodplain forests, according to a post by Gemenc Zrt. on the Pörböly Ecotourism Center’s Facebook page. Between August 28 and September 12, the company is organizing tours of the floodplain forest combined with educational presentations, during which visitors can hear the animals’ bellowing.
The excursions depart from the Pörböly Ecotourism Center at 6:30 p.m. on August 28, 29, and September 4, 5, 11, and 12. On the deer rut listening tours, visitors can not only experience, without disturbing the wildlife, the stags’ mating calls, but also gain a better understanding of this unique phenomenon through educational, interactive presentations.
Although participation in these tours is generally not recommended for children, since the tours last several hours and are only effective if visitors listen quietly throughout,
a tour specifically for children will be organized on September 12 at one of the forest railway’s stops, Lassi, where craft activities will also be available for the little ones who quickly tire of sitting quietly and listening, organizers pointed out.
Further information about the tours and registration details can be found on the Facebook page of the Gemenc Ecotourism Center.
Via MTI; Featured photo: Pexels

The letter was forwarded to MTI on Thursday by Dániel Holdosi, an activist from Szombathely. François Wakenhut was responding to an open […] The post EU Acknowledges Concerns Over Asbestos Contamination appeared first o
items.body_text:
Temporary chemical measures on affected roads must not distract from the fact that the government still lacks a genuine and transparent action plan.Continue reading
The European Commission acknowledges the seriousness of concerns over asbestos contamination in Hungary, the head of the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Environment informed Laurie Kazan-Allen, coordinator of an international organization advocating an asbestos ban. The letter was forwarded to MTI on Thursday by Dániel Holdosi, an activist from Szombathely.
François Wakenhut was responding to an open letter written in early July by 14 international anti-asbestos occupational safety, health, and environmental protection organizations and experts to the leaders of the European Union and Hungary.
In the document, they drew attention to the gravity of the situation in Szombathely, highlighting the dangers posed by the contamination, posing a particular threat to children’s health.
In a letter written on behalf of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the director-general emphasized that it is primarily the responsibility of the competent national authorities to ensure compliance with applicable EU rules in such cases, to assess the risks, and to take the necessary protective and remediation measures.
The European Commission is confident that the national authorities will continue to act swiftly and decisively to protect public health in the affected areas,”
François Wakenhut stated.
The asbestos contamination scandal broke out the day after Hungary’s parliamentary elections, when in Vas County the head of the environmental protection department at the local government office and the mayor of Szombathely announced at an emergency press conference that, in one of the city’s single-family residential areas, on several streets of the “Oladi Plateau,” crushed stone containing asbestos had been spread years earlier. Airborne asbestos fibers are seriously harmful to health.
István Orbán, director general of the government office, said that, according to reports, four quarries in Burgenland, Austria, had previously been closed due to high asbestos content, and they suspect the material may have come from there.
András Nemény, mayor of Szombathely, announced that 12 kilometers of streets in that part of the city are covered with asbestos-contaminated crushed stone, and the cost of safely removing and disposing of it exceeds the city’s financial resources.
To access the force majeure fund, he appealed to both the outgoing government and the incoming government for assistance. Tibor Navracsics, the outgoing Minister of Regional Development, promised to make the fund available, and a supporting government resolution was passed, but only the local government was able to take concrete steps; to prevent dust from spreading, they began regularly watering the affected streets and even applied a layer of bitumen to some sections, while awaiting guidance from experts on exactly what steps to take.
In the following weeks, several municipalities in Vas County—including Kőszeg, Lukácsháza, Bük, and Sárvár—reported that they might also be affected; laboratory tests revealed asbestos levels exceeding the threshold in all of these locations.
In Táplánszentkereszt, the areas in front of the daycare center, kindergarten, and school were inadvertently covered with asbestos-containing material; there, too, the local government had no other option but to spray the area with calcium chloride. In Bük, the local government had the material removed at its own expense, in compliance with regulations governing hazardous materials.
In Szombathely, weekly public forums were held; construction in the area was halted due to the imposed restrictions, and heavy vehicle traffic was temporarily banned and then restricted during certain periods.
On May 21, the Hungarian prime minister held talks in Vienna with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.

items.title: Fellőtték az űrbe a NASA új űrteleszkópját, aminek köszönhetően sokkal többet fogunk a távoli galaxisokról
items.summary: A NASA igazgatója korábban azt mondta, hogy a tervek szerint egy év alatt el tud majd végezni annyi munkát, mint amennyihez a Hubble-nek kétezer évre lett volna szüksége.
items.body_text:
Fellőtték az űrbe a NASA új űrteleszkópját, aminek köszönhetően sokkal többet fogunk a távoli galaxisokról
A terveknek megfelelően helyi idő szerint vasárnap reggel fél 8 körül útjára indították a NASA új generációs, Roman űrteleszkópját a floridai Cape Canaveral űrközpontból, körülbelül 10 perccel később pedig el is érte a pályáját, írja a CNN. A Nancy Grace Romanről, a Hubble űrtávcső egyik tervezőjéről elnevezett, mintegy 4 milliárd dollárból elkészült űrteleszkóp a SpaceX Falcon Heavy hordozórakétáján jutott a világűrbe, ahol a Földtől 1,6 millió kilométerre áll munkába – innen működik jelenleg a Webb űrteleszkóp is.
Ha minden jól megy, az új űrteleszkóp olyan nagy fényképeket tud majd készíteni távoli galaxisokról, hogy jelenleg nem létezik akkora kijelző, amin teljes méretükben elférnének. A Romannak fontos feladatai lesznek: a sötét anyag és a sötét energia vizsgálata mellett a más csillagok körül keringő exobolygókat is segíthet jobban megismerni. A küldetést öt évesre tervezték, bár a NASA szerint az űrteleszkópnak elegendő üzemanyaga lehet további öt évre is.
Első ránézésre talán nem egyszerű megmondani, hogy mi is a pláne a Roman űrtávcsőben, hiszen a fő tükre 2,4 méter átmérőjű, ami nagyjából ugyanakkora, mint a 36 éve működő Hubble-é, és jelentősen kisebb, mint a James Webb Űrteleszkóp 6,5 méteres fő tükre.
Persze a számok kontextus nélkül nem mindig adják át a teljes képet: bár a fő tükör akkora, mint a Hubble teleszkópé, a detektorai annál nagyjából százszor nagyobb területet tudnak lefedni. A NASA igazgatója, Jared Isaacman a Roman bemutatóján azt mondta, hogy a tervek szerint egy év alatt el tud majd végezni annyi munkát, mint amennyihez a Hubble-nek kétezer évre lett volna szüksége.
A Roman űrteleszkópról itt írtunk részletesebben.

items.title: Magyar Péter: Ha valaki egy neki nem tetsző személyi döntés miatt eltávolodik a Tiszától, ehhez is szíve joga van
items.summary: A miniszterelnök a kérdést lezártnak tekinti: azért, hogy ki az adott pozícióra a legmegfelelőbb jelölt, az a felelős, aki kinevezi.
items.body_text:
Magyar Péter: Ha valaki egy neki nem tetsző személyi döntés miatt eltávolodik a Tiszától, ehhez is szíve joga van
Hosszú bejegyzésben sorolta Magyar Péter a Tisza-kormány eddigi eredményeit, majd rátért a kritikus pontra, a Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatal vezetőinek kinevezésére. Azt írja, hogy teljesítették az egyik legfőbb vállalásukat, rekord idő alatt létrehozva „Európa talán legerősebb korrupcióellenes intézményét” (ehhez egyelőre az elnököt és a négyből egy elnökhelyettest neveztek ki, a hivatal felállítása csak ezután kezdődik).
„Szeretném újra világossá tenni, hogy soha nem vállaltunk olyat (és más kormány sem vállal ilyet), hogy minden vezetői pozícióra meg fogjuk a közvéleménnyel szavaztatni a jelölteket” – írta. Ezt azzal indokolta, hogy nem a közvélemény és az állampolgárok felelőssége, hogy ki az adott pozícióra a legmegfelelőbb jelölt, hanem azé, aki kinevezi.
A miniszterelnök „érzi”, hogy a demokrácia újratanulásában „lesznek döccenők, akár néha személyes csalódások is”, de a személyek kinevezéséért a megválasztott vezető a felelős, „nem egy influenszer, nem egy volt politikus és nem is a közvélemény többsége. Ha mindig a közvélemény döntene kinevezésekről, jogszabályokról, költségvetésről, adókról, akkor az ország kormányozhatatlanná válna.”
Ezután védelmébe vette a képviselőit, akik szerinte mindent a hazájuknak rendeltek alá, és minden döntést ennek tudatában hoznak meg, akkor is, ha az adott pillanatban ez nem tűnik népszerűnek. „Lehet ezért minket kritizálni, lehet velünk egyet nem érteni” – ismételte meg a többször megfogalmazott állítást, hozzátéve, hogy a lelkiismeretük tiszta, nálunk jobban senki nem szeretné az elsíbolt állami vagyonok visszaszerzését és a felelősök megbüntetését.
Végül ismét a tiszás közösségnek üzent, a péntekinél egy fokkal keményebben:
„Természetesen ha valaki a 110 napos kormányzásunk eredményei mellett egy neki nem tetsző személyi döntés miatt eltávolodik a Tiszától, ehhez is szíve joga van” – írta. Majd hozzátette, hogy ők semmilyen nyomásra nem fognak engedni a vállalásaikból, és pontot tett az ügy végére: „Részemről a kérdés a fentiek szerint lezárva”.
Pénteken a hivatal elnöke a Telex stúdiójában járt, megválasztása után először a Telexnek adott videós interjút. „Tudom, hogy mindenki az elszámoltatást várja, tudom, hogy mindenki a bilincsek kattanását várja, és tudom, hogy mindenki szeretné hallani a zörgő rácsokat, de létre kell hozni a hivatalt, meg kell választani még három elnökhelyettest” – mondta Unger Anna, akit pénteken titkos szavazáson választott meg az Országgyűlés a Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatal (NVVH) élére.
Unger azt ígérte, a következő hetekben azon lesz, hogy megtalálja a legjobb munkatársakat az elnökhelyettesekkel együttműködve minden lehetséges pozícióra.

items.summary: A 208 GT lágy hibrid segédhajtással és 145 lóerős összteljesítménnyel, a Seat Ibiza FR pedig segédhajtás nélkül, de négyhengeres, 150 lóerős motorral lóg ki a hasonló kategóriás autók sorából. Mindkettő kompromisszumos megoldás, a szerethetőségük pedig éppen ezen múlhat.
items.body_text:
Remek játékok felnőtteknek, de tényleg érdemes ilyen sokat költeni a Seat és a Peugeot erős kisautóira?
Ezt a cikket a Telex és az autóMAGAZIN együttműködésének keretében olvashatják.
A kisautók kategóriáját egyszerre számolja fel a típusok folyamatos méretnövekedése, illetve az, hogy a gyártók nem tudnak elég nagy hasznot bezsebelni az eleve olcsónak szánt konstrukciókkal, miközben emelniük kell az árakat a növekvő fejlesztési és gyártási költségek miatt. Szintén a hagyományos hajtású kisautók terepét szűkíti, hogy rontják a flottaszintű károsanyag-kibocsátást, amire minden Európában jelenlévő márkának fokozottan ügyelnie kell, ha nem akar büntetést fizetni.
Emiatt válik érdekessé, hogy a Seat nyolc évnyi gyártás után mégis áldozott egy kis pénzt az Ibiza frissítésére. Újfajta audiorendszerre, más beltéri anyagokra, valamivel több puha tapintású felületre és hangulatvilágításra számíthat, aki beül a most kapható új Ibizába. A jelenlegi Polóhoz konstrukciós szempontból hasonló, azonos platformra épülő ötödik generációs Ibiza felújított verzióját kívülről a módosított hűtőmaszkjáról, a karakteresebb lökhárítóiról és az élesebb kontúrú LED-fényszóróiról könnyű felismerni.
A futómű, a kormányzás és a motorválaszték is változatlan. Ez azt is jelenti, hogy a klasszikus 1,5 literes, négyhengeres, 150 lóerős turbós benzinmotor (TSI) is játékban marad, mivel teljesíti az Euro 7 környezetvédelmi normát. Ez azért jó hír, mert az Ibiza továbbra is elég könnyű autó, alig több mint 1,2 tonnát nyom, miközben több mint 4 méter hosszú.

A Volkswagen-konszern más DSG-váltóihoz képest szinte minden helyzetben nagyon gyorsan, rántások nélkül, előrelátóan dolgozik az Ibiza váltója. Ennek megfelelően egyenletes és közvetlen a teljesítményleadás, egészen a nagyon magas, 216 km/órás végsebességig. Jók a gyorsulási értékek is, az Ibiza FR álló helyzetből 7,9 másodperc alatt gyorsul 100 km/órára.
Ezzel elektromos segítség nélkül is simán lehagyja a Peugeot-t, ami 8,4 másodperc alatt éri el ezt a tempót, és legfeljebb kétszázig gyorsíthatjuk. Mégsem léphetünk tovább kritika nélkül a lelkes négyhengeresről, mivel lényegesen több benzint fogyaszt a francia háromhengeresnél. A gazdaságos vezetéssel teljesített tesztkörön a Seat 5,5 liter benzint kért száz kilométerre, a teszt összesített átlaga pedig 6,5 liter volt, ami mindkét esetben fél literrel múlta felül a 208-as átlagfogyasztását.

A 208 GT 48 voltos hibrid segédhajtásának villanymotorját a hatfokozatú dupla kuplungos váltóba építették. Teljesítménye 15,6 kilowatt 51 newtonméter csúcsnyomaték mellett, ami sima és lendületes elindulást tesz lehetővé. A 208-as sajnos csak alkalmanként hajlandó leállítani a belső égésű motorját, és teljesen a villanymotor erejére hagyatkozni. A kétféle hajtás összekapcsolása néha szépen és zökkenőmentesen működik, máskor kevésbé.
A hajtáslánc motorféküzemben folyamatosan visszatáplál és sosem vitorlázik, ez kissé rontja a folyamatos haladást, de valóban hatékony. Autópályán, tempósabb haladásnál elviselhető motorbúgással békít ki, miközben az Ibiza 1.5 TSI motorja magasabb fordulatszámon a hangosabb konstrukciók közé tartozik. items.body_text:
Foreign Pupils on the Rise in Czech Schools - Nearly One in Five in Prague
Prague Morning
Of the nearly one million pupils attending Czech primary schools last academic year, almost 8% were foreign nationals, most commonly from Ukraine.
According to the Czech Statistical Office (CSO), Prague recorded the highest proportion, with foreign pupils making up 18% of all children in its primary schools.
Compulsory education is mandatory for Czech citizens as well as citizens of other European Union member states who reside in the Czech Republic for more than 90 days. The requirement also applies to foreign nationals with long-term residence permits.
Their children therefore have the same rights as Czech children, including access to free education, school meals and extracurricular activities.
The number of foreign pupils increased significantly after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, nearly doubling that year. Their numbers have continued to rise ever since. Today, children from Ukraine account for 5% of all pupils in the Czech Republic.
The trend is similar in secondary schools, where the proportion of foreign pupils reached its highest level in the past 10 years, at almost 5% of the total.
Although the number of children in primary schools has remained relatively stable at just over one million in recent years, a sharp decline is expected in the coming years due to the falling birth rate, according to Vendula Kašparová of the CSO’s Social Development Statistics Department. The office said the birth rate has been falling continuously for the fifth consecutive year.
The decline is already visible at the kindergarten level. The number of children enrolled in kindergartens fell below 350,000 in the 2025/2026 academic year, the first time this has happened since 2013. Over the past three years, enrolment has dropped by more than 21,000 children, or around 5.8%.
Fewer Children Receiving Deferrals From Starting School
Kašparová identifies another clear trend: fewer children are being granted deferrals from starting compulsory school. Since the 2021/2022 academic year, the proportion of six-year-olds whose school entry was deferred has fallen from 24.1% in September 2021 to 17.7% in September 2025, representing just under 21,000 pupils.
Furthermore, an amendment to the Education Act is expected to reduce the number of deferrals even further. Under the new rules, deferrals will only be granted when justified by a medical condition that prevents a child from attending school.
This could include a serious medical condition following surgery, cancer treatment or a moderate intellectual disability.

items.body_text:
Czechia, the Land of Burgers. More Fast Food Chains Enter the Market
Prague Morning
The Czech fast food market is expanding beyond its established players, with new international brands entering the country and existing chains opening restaurants in smaller cities.
McDonald’s and KFC continue to build their networks, while brands from Germany, the United States and Poland are looking for opportunities in the Czech Republic.
The expansion is increasingly moving beyond Prague and other major cities, with retail parks becoming an important location for new restaurants.
Burgermeister prepares Czech debut
One of the newest international brands preparing to enter the Czech market is Germany’s Burgermeister. The Berlin-based burger chain plans to open its first restaurant on Wenceslas Square at the beginning of next year.
The company already sees its Prague location as more than a single restaurant. It is also considering further locations across the country.
Popeyes and Burger King continue expanding
Burger King entered the Czech market 18 years ago and now operates around 70 restaurants. Popeyes arrived much later but has expanded quickly, opening 19 locations during its first three years in the country.
The companies are building a network that stretches from smaller regional towns to central Prague. In Králův Dvůr, a town of around 11,000 people, both Burger King and Popeyes operate at the Litavka Retail Park.
Popeyes is preparing additional restaurants at the Eden shopping centre and in the Budějovická area of Prague. The chain is also expanding into regional cities, with planned locations in Klatovy and Písek.
Five Guys adds another international brand
The Czech burger market gained another major international name last December when U.S. chain Five Guys opened its first Prague restaurant.
The restaurant is located in the former Máj department store on Národní Street. Five Guys is known for burgers prepared to order and a wide range of toppings, allowing customers to customise their meals.
Its prices, however, are generally higher than those of traditional fast food chains.
Another U.S. brand, Dave’s Hot Chicken, is also expected to enter the Czech market this year, according to consulting firm Cushman & Wakefield.
The chain specialises in spicy fried chicken and will therefore compete directly with established players such as KFC and Popeyes.
Czech chains are looking beyond their home cities
The expansion is not limited to international companies.
Czech burger chain Mama’s Burger is also developing its network. Originally based in Ostrava, the company has expanded into several larger Czech cities and operates a restaurant at Prague’s Arkády Pankrác shopping centre.
The company is also seeking franchise partners as it looks to increase the number of locations.

items.body_text:
Slavia Prague to Face Bayern Munich, Arsenal and Porto in Champions League
Prague Morning
Slavia Prague have learned their eight opponents for the 2026/27 UEFA Champions League league phase following Thursday’s draw in Monaco.
Slavia will play four matches at home at Eden Arena and four away.
At home, Slavia will welcome Arsenal, Aston Villa, Villarreal and Lens. Their away fixtures will take them to Bayern Munich, Porto, Fenerbahçe and Sabah Baku in Azerbaijan.
The most high-profile home fixture will be against Arsenal, the reigning Premier League champions. Slavia also faced the London club in last season’s Champions League campaign, making the return meeting at Eden Arena particularly notable.
The toughest away assignment is likely to come in Munich, where Slavia will face six-time European champions Bayern at the Allianz Arena. The team will also travel to Portugal to meet Porto and to Istanbul for a match against Fenerbahçe.
The longest trip of the league phase will be to Baku to face Azerbaijani champions Sabah, who are making their debut in the Champions League league phase.
How the Champions League league phase works
The 2026/27 competition is being played under UEFA’s new league-phase format for the third consecutive season. Instead of a traditional group stage, all 36 teams are placed in one league table.
Each club plays eight matches against eight different opponents, with two opponents drawn from each of the four seeding pots. Every team has four home and four away games.
The top eight teams in the final standings will advance directly to the round of 16. Teams finishing ninth to 24th will enter a knockout playoff for the remaining eight places, while clubs finishing from 25th to 36th will be eliminated.
The league phase begins on September 8–10, with six rounds taking place before the end of 2026. The final two matchdays will be played in January, with the league phase concluding on January 27. UEFA will announce the exact dates and kick-off times for each individual match later.

items.body_text:
Two Arrested Over Drugs Within Probe Into Abkhaz Blogger’s Death, Police Say
Two people were arrested over the purchase and storage of drugs within a probe into the death of Abkhaz blogger Daur Buava, the Interior Ministry said on August 30, adding that one of the suspects gave drugs to Buava’s female friend, who used them with Buava before leaving him in a life-threatening condition.
According to the Ministry, the arrests followed searches in two homes in Tbilisi conducted “based on the circumstances established within the investigation into Daur Buava’s death,” during which “various types of narcotic drugs — marijuana and methadone — packaged in 10 packets were seized as evidence.”
The investigation and questioning established that both suspects were acquainted with Buava and his woman friend, the ministry said, adding that one of the suspects “gave a narcotic substance free of charge” to the woman.
The woman “used the narcotic substance with Daur Buava and then left him in a life-threatening condition without approaching anyone for help,” the Ministry noted.
The arrests came a day after a foreign national woman was arrested on accusations of abandoning Buava in a “critical” and life-threatening condition without seeking help after using drugs with him in a Tbilisi apartment. Buava’s lawyer, Natia Mezvrishvili, later told the media that the woman is a Ukrainian national, and that Buava’s friends and defense do not share the version of drug-related death and plan an alternative forensic study.
Buava was found dead in the apartment on August 27, reportedly days after his suspected death, after neighbors were alerted by a strong odor. The Interior Ministry said a preliminary inspection of the body found no signs of violence.
Buava, known on TikTok as Tarielovich and followed by more than 100,000 people, was born in Tkvarcheli, occupied Abkhazia, and moved to Georgia proper in 2021, where he was granted Georgian citizenship under a simplified procedure in 2022. He lived in Tbilisi-controlled territory and published videos promoting Abkhaz-Georgian friendship.
In 2022, the de facto security service of Sokhumi filed charges of high treason against Buava, saying the blogger published videos with “direct and latent appeals to an unlimited circle of users aimed at damaging sovereignty, territorial integrity, national security and defense capacity.”

Police Arrest Foreign National on Allegations of Abandoning Abkhaz Blogger Daur Buava in Danger
The Georgian Interior Ministry announced the arrest of a foreign national in connection with Abkhaz blogger Daur Buava’s death, noting the accused abandoned Buava in “critical and life-threatening condition” after the two took a narcotic substance in a Tbilisi apartment. The Ministry did not disclose the name or the nationality of the accused.
According to the Ministry, the investigation shows that Buava and the suspect, who were friends, “were together at Daur Buava’s temporary residence in Tbilisi, Didi Dighomi, where they used a narcotic substance, after which both of them became unwell.” The Ministry said that questioning established that the suspect left Buava, who was “in a critical and life-threatening condition,” alone.
“Specifically, the accused locked the door of the apartment from the outside using a second key and left the scene without informing anyone about what had happened or approaching anyone to seek help for Daur Buava,” the Ministry said.
According to the Ministry’s statement, an investigation is underway under Articles 115 and 128 of the Criminal Code, covering incitement to suicide [a standard provision when a person is found dead in unclear circumstances in Georgia], and abandoning a person in danger.
On August 28, reports emerged that Buava, a 31-year-old Abkhaz blogger and TikToker who lived in Tbilisi-controlled territory and published videos promoting Abkhaz-Georgian friendship, was found dead in Tbilisi.
His body was reportedly discovered in a Tbilisi apartment on August 27, days after his suspected death, after neighbors raised concerns over a strong odor. The Interior Ministry said a preliminary inspection of the body found no signs of violence.
Buava, known on TikTok as Tarielovich and followed by more than 100,000 people, was born in Tkvarcheli, occupied Abkhazia, and moved to Georgia proper in 2021, where he was granted Georgian citizenship under a simplified procedure in 2022. He lived in Tbilisi-controlled territory and published videos promoting Abkhaz-Georgian friendship.
In 2022, the de facto security service of Sokhumi filed charges of high treason against Buava, saying the blogger published videos with “direct and latent appeals to an unlimited circle of users aimed at damaging sovereignty, territorial integrity, national security and defense capacity.”

items.body_text:
Orchards, Roads Damaged as Rains Cause Flooding in Imereti
Heavy rains on August 27 damaged orchards, crops, and roads in the western Georgian region of Imereti, with the damage particularly affecting neighborhoods and villages in Baghdati Municipality.
Videos from the scene show streams of water rushing through roads and orchards and entering homes, with locals saying the rains caused small rivers to swell suddenly. Residents are seen struggling to protect their houses, yards and belongings, while appealing to the authorities for assistance.
“In just half an hour, this small river wreaked havoc on all my family’s work,” a resident of Obcha village of Baghdati municipality wrote on social media, posting videos of the orchard filled by rapidly moving water and a flooded house. “I have no words. I walk around in tears.”
Local media also published an image showing a section of a forest-covered slope that had collapsed.
Heavy flooding was also reported in villages in nearby Zestaphoni Municipality, while rainwater flooded streets in Kutaisi, the region’s administrative center.
The Baghdati Municipality City Hall said authorities are operating in emergency mode, and a commission has been set up to assess the damage. Hundreds of households have been left without gas and electricity.

items.title: Asbestos allegedly found under Rustaveli Avenue during renovation
items.summary: The Public Defender’s Office has urged the authorities to verify the reports.
items.body_text:
Georgia’s Public Defender’s Office has issued a warning, calling on Tbilisi City Hall to investigate the presence of asbestos allegedly found under Rustaveli Avenue during ongoing rehabilitation work.
The agency issued its appeal after pictures of what appears to be asbestos found on Rustaveli Avenue surfaced online on 21 August. Social media user Irakli Pipia said that asbestos was used by the Soviet authorities to construct water pipes under the thoroughfare.
On Thursday, urban and environmental activist Nata Peradze said that samples of the shattered asbestos pipes were collected and are ready to be sent to a laboratory in Berlin. She added that they need to raise funds for the analysis.
The Public Defender of Georgia issued its appeal on Facebook on Thursday.
‘Asbestos is a substance with high health risk and its exposure is related to serious diseases, including mesothelioma and lung cancer. The risk increases sharply during mechanical exposure, cutting, crushing, drilling and removal from the ground.’
‘International standards for asbestos regulation have not been fully implemented in Georgia, technical regulations have not been adopted that would regulate the protection of employees from exposure to asbestos in the workplace’, the agency said.
It also warned that schools located around the avenue will start their classes on 15 September, and that students could potentially be exposed to asbestos.
‘Children are a particularly vulnerable group to asbestos exposure, as their respiratory system is still in the process of formation, and the latent period of asbestos-related diseases lasts for decades.’
The Public Defender called on Tbilisi City hall to determine whether the material found in the renovation area contains asbestos, and to spread awareness about the matter.
In 2019, more than 70,000 people in the EU died from past exposure to asbestos at work.
Authorities have been discussing the renovation of Rustaveli Avenue since 2023. The renovation started in late July, 2026 with authorities saying it is scheduled to be finished in November.
The construction company responsible for the rehabilitation work has been fined four times for failing to adhere to the stipulated work schedule, leading to a total of ₾5,000 ($1,900) in fines.
Rustaveli Avenue has historically been the site of numerous mass protests and clashes between protesters and riot police.

items.title: Lavrov says Armenia must choose between EU and EAEU
items.summary: Lavrov also criticised Yerevan for its handling of Russia’s concession over Armenia’s railways.
items.body_text:
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has said Armenia must choose between the EU and its membership in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), echoing previous remarks issued by other Russian officials.
Lavrov’s remarks reflect the deepening standoff between the two countries. Armenia pushes towards EU integration, which Russia sees as incompatible with EAEU membership. Pashinyan also wants to restructure the ownership of the Russia-run national railway over concerns about deterring foreign investments. Those two issues together highlight Armenia’s effort to balance its relationship with historical partner Russia while pivoting towards the West.
On Armenia’s EU aspirations, Lavrov said that Pashinyan’s position, that a referendum on EU membership can only be discussed after Armenia submits its application and drafts a ‘road map’, shows that he does not fully ‘trust his own people’ to make an honest choice. Lavrov recalled that in May, EAEU countries called on Armenia to hold a referendum to decide whether to stay with the EAEU or join the EU, which he said is a justified request.
‘The norms of one organisation are incompatible with the norms of the other organisation. This has been said many times’, Lavrov said.
Lavrov argued that Armenia now has to choose between the EU and what it already has, pointing to trade turnover which he said exceeded $6 billion in the past three years and had reached $12 billion in one year. He did not specify whether he meant trade between Armenia and the EAEU or with Russia.
Turning to the railway issue, Lavrov stressed that Russia has done everything for its part to normalise relations with Armenia, and expressed surprise that Armenia discusses the railway concession publicly rather than directly with its partner.
Armenia’s railway system is owned by Russian Railways (RZhD) under a 30-year concession signed in 2008.
Earlier in August, Pashinyan told reporters that Armenia is seeking to negotiate a compromise with Russia over the Russian-run national railway, rather than unilaterally cancelling Russian Railways’ (RZhD) management contract. Pashinyan first called for ending the RZhD’s presence in February, arguing that Russian control discourages investment from international partners. In July, he threatened arbitration and a $2 billion annual bill for RZhD’s management rights, triggering warnings from Russia.
The Russian Foreign Ministry, in response, has accused the West of ‘blackmailing’ Armenia over the concession of the railway.
‘They demand the removal of the “Russian factor” from the transport sector, while in return promising multimillion-dollar investments and access to projects whose economic viability is hardly apparent’, the Russian ministry said.
During a press briefing on Thursday, Pashinyan said Armenia expressed its positions on Russia and its security bloc, the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO), ‘in a transparent, public, and honest manner’.
Armenia’s membership in the CSTO has also been called into question by Russia. Yerevan ‘froze’ its membership in the bloc in early 2024, with Pashinyan on Monday saying resuming Armenia’s membership in the CSTO was not in his government’s five-year plan.
‘I would be very happy if the organisation decided to expel Armenia from the CSTO. It would free us from the dilemma of whether or not to withdraw’, he said at the time.

items.title: Azerbaijan calls on Russia to investigate protest in front of its embassy in Moscow
items.summary: Baku described the protest as an ‘ugly and biased campaign’ against Azerbaijan.
items.body_text:
Azerbaijan has called on Russia to investigate three National Bolsheviks for putting up banners on the walls of the Azerbaijani Embassy in Moscow calling for the release of Russians detained in Azerbaijan. Baku has called the incident an ‘unacceptable provocation’.
Footage from the small protest appeared on a Telegram channel linked to the National Bolshevik Movement. In the video, the protesters criticised Azerbaijan for launching criminal cases against Russians.
Their banners read: ‘Azerbaijan’s State Security Service tortures, [Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev] covers it up!, ‘Russian blood is on your hands!’, and ‘Let the Russian citizens go!’.
The movement said that Azerbaijan ‘consistently pursues an anti-Russian policy’.
A few hours later Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry issued an official statement saying that the incident might be aimed ‘at artificially straining Azerbaijani-Russian relations’.
The ministry described the protest as an ‘ugly and biased campaign’ against Azerbaijan, which it claimed was being waged in certain Russian media outlets.
On 19 August, Azerbaijan Prosecutor General’s Office issued warrants for three Russian citizens accusing them of making calls to overthrow the government.
Relations between Azerbaijan and Russia deteriorated following the crash of an Azerbaijan Airlines passenger plane shot down in Grozny in December 2024, which resulted in the deaths of 38 people.
Russia subsequently arrested Azerbaijanis, accusing them of crimes committed as far back as the early 2000s; Azerbaijan characterized these actions as an instance of ethnic discrimination.
The arrests of Azerbaijanis in Russia were followed by the arrests of Russian citizens in Azerbaijan in June.

items.title: Ex-President Niinistö: Norway's late King Harald was a 'wise elder'
items.summary: Harald had a positive view of Finland.
items.body_text:
Finnish politicians are reacting to the passing of the Norwegian king, Harald V, who died on Friday.
His successor, Crown Prince Haakon, immediately ascended the throne.
Norway's government on Friday declared a period of national mourning, which will continue until the king's funeral.
President Alexander Stubb expressed his condolences on the death of Harald in a post on X.
European Parliament member Anna-Maja Henriksson meanwhile said she shares the grief of the Norwegian people and the royal family.
President Niinistö pays warm tribute
Former Finnish President Sauli Niinistö described the late King Harald of Norway as a wise leader.
"He was not only a king but also a very good-humoured person," Niinistö told Yle in an interview.
Niinistö said the king was a "wise elder" who knew how to make his views count.
"He was very easy to talk to about a wide range of subjects, and he also used a lot of humour."
Harald had a very positive view of Finland, and Nordic cooperation was important to him. Their conversations sometimes touched on historical events as well.
Niinistö and King Harald met around ten times over the years at international gatherings.
"King Harald lived for his nation and its success. And now that nation carries on," Niinistö said.

items.title: Iceland votes 'No' to resuming EU talks
items.summary: Iceland voted 'No' to resuming membership negotiations with the European Union, final referendum results showed Sunday, dealing a heavy blow to Brussels which had been keen to welcome a new wealthy member.
items.body_text:
In a vote held Saturday, 52.8 percent of Icelanders rejected the resumption of EU entry talks suspended 13 years ago, while 47.2 percent voted 'Yes', according to the official tally published by RUV, the public broadcaster.
The result will be a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues to facilitate Iceland's accession.
The result will also likely bury the EU question in Iceland until at least 2028.
The country of just under 400,000 people applied to join the EU in the wake of a 2009 financial crisis that devastated its economy.
Membership talks were then suspended in 2013 when a eurosceptic government came to power.
Amid growing international tensions, Iceland's current government headed by Social Democratic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir wanted to sound out Icelanders on deepening their ties to the EU.
READ ALSO: As Iceland votes on the EU, which countries could be next to join?
The small North Atlantic island is already closely linked to the EU as a member of the European Economic Area and the free-movement Schengen zone -- ties which will remain unchanged.
Technically, the referendum result is non-binding but the government has vowed to respect it.
The government will hold a press conference on Sunday at 1:00 pm (1300 GMT) to present its plans.
'We will be fine'
Debates ahead of the vote had mainly revolved around domestic and economic issues, even if the war in Ukraine and US President Donald Trump's ambitions for neighbouring Greenland -- which he has mixed up with Iceland on several occasions -- featured in discussions.
The campaign had "lifted discussions about the EU, about Iceland's place in the world, about our general geopolitical situation and status, to a higher level", Frostadottir said on Saturday after she cast her ballot.
She was openly in favour of a 'Yes', but "we will be fine also if it's a 'No'," she said.
Frostadottir had vowed that if Iceland rejected the resumption of entry talks, the EU membership issue would not be put back on the political agenda during her mandate, which ends in 2028.
The government had also said that in the event of a 'No', it would leave to parliament the question of whether or not to formally withdraw the country's EU membership application.
Political analysts had said they did not expect the government to resign in the event of a 'No' victory. Made up of three parties with differing views on EU membership, it could emerge weakened by a rejection.
Had the 'Yes' camp emerged victorious, Iceland would have resumed its negotiations with Brussels, including on the hotly contested issue of fishing -- a pillar of Iceland's economy and part of its national identity, and over which Reykjavik wants to retain exclusive control.
Any accession agreement would have then been put to a new referendum in Iceland.
The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc -- 90 percent of companies in the industry are against the idea -- and the EU had tried to woo them with a conciliatory approach ahead of the vote.
"Iceland's unique specificities on fisheries and agriculture are well known. They would have to be carefully considered," EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos had said.
"I'm confident that, together with EU member states, we would find creative solutions."
An EU source in Brussels told AFP: "I don't think anyone (in the EU) wants to block an accession over a question of fish."
Brussels had hoped to be able to present Icelandic membership as an example of positive enlargement that could also make it more palatable for member states to agree to take in poorer countries like Montenegro.
It would also have enabled it to enlarge its presence in the strategic Arctic region, and perhaps helped change some minds in ultra-wealthy non-EU member Norway.

items.title: Election day and new deportation rules: What changes in Sweden in September?
items.summary: Stricter rules on deportation for foreigners who commit crimes are coming into force – and election day is here. Let's take a look at what changes in Sweden in September 2026.
items.body_text:
Stricter rules on deportation for foreigners who commit crimes
Starting September 1st, it will be easier for foreigners in Sweden who have committed crimes to be deported. Committing a crime – in cases when the imposed penalty is more severe than a fine – was already generally grounds for deportation, so these rules will make it even easier.
It will do this in a number of ways, including: the court will no longer take into account obstacles to enforcement when considering whether deportation should take place; prosecutors will be obliged to request deportation when a foreigner is charged with a crime that is grounds for deportation; the restriction on deportation of foreigners who came to Sweden before the age of 15 will be abolished; re-entry bans have been extended and in more cases may be indefinite; and penalties have been increased for certain crimes under the Aliens Act.
Sweden tests new mobile emergency alert system
Sweden is set to test its new mobile emergency alert system, called SE-Alert, in Stockholm and Gotland on September 7th. The test will take place at 3pm alongside the quarterly outdoor emergency siren "Hesa Fredrik".
This means that if you are in the Stockholm area or Gotland, have an up-to-date smartphone which is switched on and connected to a mobile network, you will receive a pop-up text notification accompanied by a loud audio signal and vibration, even if you've got your phone on silent. It's just a test and you don't need to do anything – but it will be sent out to everyone, including children, the elderly and international tourists who just happen to be in the area at the time of the test, so it's worth informing friends and family members of the test in advance if you think they may otherwise get concerned or caught off guard by receiving the notification.
It will be sent out to everyone in the area regardless of whether you have a Swedish or international number, the Swedish Civil Defence and Resilience Agency – which is responsible for the test – confirmed to The Local.
You don't have to download an app to receive the notification, it will happen automatically. It's also worth knowing that if you're in Stockholm's neighbouring regions such as Uppsala, Södermanland or Västmanland, you may also receive the test alert (or you may not), because is because it's sent out using cell broadcast, so it depends on the signal range rather than exact administrative regional borders.
For this first test, the header may be in English. The message itself will be in Swedish followed by English.
SE-Alert will be tested nationwide in December.
Election Day
Advanced voting opens on August 26th, but September 13th is the official voting day when polling stations will be open around the country and many Swedes will go to cast their vote. Sweden holds its elections for the national parliament as well as regional councils and municipal councils on the same day. Remember that even if you're not a Swedish citizen, you may have the right to vote in the regional and local elections.
The result usually comes in at some point late in the evening. We'll of course be covering it live here on The Local.
Pay your residual tax
If you received your final tax statement (slutskattebesked) in June, you have to pay any residual tax by September 14th.
If your outstanding tax is under 100 kronor you don't need to pay it back until it reaches 100 kronor or over, and if you received your final tax declaration later than June, your deadline will also be later.
You can find out all the relevant details on the Tax Agency's tax repayment page.
New interest rate update
Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, is set to announce its next decision on the interest rate on September 24th. It is widely expected to raise the interest rate at some point before the end of the year (in fact, many experts had predicted a hike would come in August), the question is just when. items.title: Five tips to get your hands on a first-hand rental apartment in Sweden
items.summary: They're often high quality and cheaper than the market rate, but oh so hard to come by. The Local's readers share their best tips for how foreigners without years in the housing queue can rent a so-called first-hand apartment in Sweden.
items.body_text:
Sweden's tightly-regulated rental market means that most newcomers end up moving from one sublet apartment (or "second-hand apartment" as it's usually known in Sweden even among English-speakers, andrahandslägenhet) to the next every year or so.
In practice rents are often high and leases insecure, despite laws in theory preventing overpriced sublets.
First-hand rentals, on the other hand, tend to be better quality, more long-term and often remarkably cheap, making them an attractive but elusive option – unless you signed up for the public housing queue years, or even decades, ago it's hard to snag one.
But not impossible. In a Facebook post, The Local's readers shared their tips for how they managed to beat the competition and secure a first-hand rental.
Here are their best strategies:
1. Move out of the big cities
Many readers suggested avoiding Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö, where the housing shortage is particularly bad. Student cities like Uppsala and Lund also tend to be on that list, but many smaller or more rural municipalities have far shorter housing queues, sometimes none at all.
“I live in a 10,000 people city, 180 kilometres from Stockholm,” said Rodrigo.
Johanna said she’s moved from Stockholm to the countryside, adding she’s got “many friends living in more rural areas of Heby and Dalarna or way up north like Haparanda” where apartments come “dirt cheap”.
2. You don’t always have to move far
If you can put up with a longer commute, there are many municipalities within commuting distance of the big cities which have shorter housing queues and reasonable public transport connections.
“On any given day we have 100 different rental flats here in Eskilstuna – it’s literally one hour’s train ride to Stockholm,” said Jörgen.
3. Keep an eye out for exceptions
Some housing queues make exceptions from their standard housing queue for certain categories of apartments.
These vary depending on the municipality, but could include for example new builds. In Stockholm, there’s a special category called “bostadssnabben” which are apartments offered on a first-come, first-served basis, regardless of how many queue points the applicants have.
READ ALSO:
Some municipalities also allow tenants to swap apartments internally, so you may be able to go for the low hanging fruit initially and then later find someone who wants to swap apartments with you.
4. Get in the queue anyway
It’s not uncommon for people to sign up for rental queues even if they’re not thinking of moving any time soon – many Swedes sign up as soon as they turn 18, and even many property owners stay in the queue – in order to collect queue points and improve their chances of renting in the future.
Not all municipalities charge a fee for a spot in the housing queue, either, so it may even be worth having a think about in which areas of Sweden you might conceivably want to live at some point in the future, and signing up for those queues on the off-chance that you end up moving there.
Far from everyone in the queue is active, and sometimes, all you need is a bit of luck.
“Be very active. Apply to as many as you can, as often as you can. Don’t be too selective about the area. I got one where the primary applicant had to have 70 percent of the income. Less competition,” said Marios, who got a 90 square metre apartment in a Stockholm suburb in three months.
5. Go private
The most common way of renting in Sweden is through the municipalities’ own housing agencies, and in some queues such as Stockholm, private landlords rent out their homes via these queues too.
But in some cities, there are private companies that rent out apartments outside of the housing queue, and they don’t always follow the same “queue point” procedure as the municipality. Some have their own housing queue, which may be shorter, and some use a lottery system, for example.

items.title: Iceland votes 'No' to resuming EU talks
items.summary: Iceland voted 'No' to resuming membership negotiations with the European Union, final referendum results showed Sunday, dealing a heavy blow to Brussels which had been keen to welcome a new wealthy member.
items.body_text:
In a vote held Saturday, 52.8 percent of Icelanders rejected the resumption of EU entry talks suspended 13 years ago, while 47.2 percent voted 'Yes', according to the official tally published by RUV, the public broadcaster.
The result will be a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues to facilitate Iceland's accession.
The result will also likely bury the EU question in Iceland until at least 2028.
The country of just under 400,000 people applied to join the EU in the wake of a 2009 financial crisis that devastated its economy.
Membership talks were then suspended in 2013 when a eurosceptic government came to power.
Amid growing international tensions, Iceland's current government headed by Social Democratic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir wanted to sound out Icelanders on deepening their ties to the EU.
READ ALSO: As Iceland votes on the EU, which countries could be next to join?
The small North Atlantic island is already closely linked to the EU as a member of the European Economic Area and the free-movement Schengen zone -- ties which will remain unchanged.
Technically, the referendum result is non-binding but the government has vowed to respect it.
The government will hold a press conference on Sunday at 1:00 pm (1300 GMT) to present its plans.
'We will be fine'
Debates ahead of the vote had mainly revolved around domestic and economic issues, even if the war in Ukraine and US President Donald Trump's ambitions for neighbouring Greenland -- which he has mixed up with Iceland on several occasions -- featured in discussions.
The campaign had "lifted discussions about the EU, about Iceland's place in the world, about our general geopolitical situation and status, to a higher level", Frostadottir said on Saturday after she cast her ballot.
She was openly in favour of a 'Yes', but "we will be fine also if it's a 'No'," she said.
Frostadottir had vowed that if Iceland rejected the resumption of entry talks, the EU membership issue would not be put back on the political agenda during her mandate, which ends in 2028.
The government had also said that in the event of a 'No', it would leave to parliament the question of whether or not to formally withdraw the country's EU membership application.
Political analysts had said they did not expect the government to resign in the event of a 'No' victory. Made up of three parties with differing views on EU membership, it could emerge weakened by a rejection.
Had the 'Yes' camp emerged victorious, Iceland would have resumed its negotiations with Brussels, including on the hotly contested issue of fishing -- a pillar of Iceland's economy and part of its national identity, and over which Reykjavik wants to retain exclusive control.
Any accession agreement would have then been put to a new referendum in Iceland.
The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc -- 90 percent of companies in the industry are against the idea -- and the EU had tried to woo them with a conciliatory approach ahead of the vote.
"Iceland's unique specificities on fisheries and agriculture are well known. They would have to be carefully considered," EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos had said.
"I'm confident that, together with EU member states, we would find creative solutions."
An EU source in Brussels told AFP: "I don't think anyone (in the EU) wants to block an accession over a question of fish."
Brussels had hoped to be able to present Icelandic membership as an example of positive enlargement that could also make it more palatable for member states to agree to take in poorer countries like Montenegro.
It would also have enabled it to enlarge its presence in the strategic Arctic region, and perhaps helped change some minds in ultra-wealthy non-EU member Norway.
