items.body_text:
Boat with around 270 people on board capsizes off North Cyprus; one dead
NICOSIA, Aug 30 - One person died after a boat with around 270 people on board capsized off North Cyprus on Sunday, Turkish Cypriot media reported.
Turkish Cypriot Transport Minister Erhan Arikli told Anadolu that one passenger had died when the ferry capsized. He said there were 267 people on board, 259 of whom were passengers and eight of whom were crew.
The privately owned ferry left the North Cyprus port of Kyrenia at 12:30 p.m. (0930 GMT) and immediately started taking on water for an unknown reason, Turkey's state-run news agency Anadolu reported.
It was heading for the Turkish port of Tasucu in Mersin province in the eastern Mediterranean.
Those rescued from the vessel were taken to Kyrenia port to be transferred to hospitals, he added.
Murat Senkul, the mayor of Kyrenia, told broadcaster CNN Turk that 159 passengers on board the vessel had been reached.
Video footage showed people in red life jackets sitting or standing on top of the overturned vessel as authorities scrambled coastguard and private vessels for assistance to bring them to shore.
The Kibris newspaper reported that the vessel, which some reports said was a catamaran, began taking in water about four miles off the shore. REUTERS

items.body_text:
Austria sees record number of heat-related deaths in June and July
- Austria recorded a historic high of 646 heat-related deaths in June and July, surpassing the previous record of 570 in the same months of 2024.
- The rise in deaths is linked to intense and frequent heatwaves caused by human-made climate change, with Europe being the fastest-warming continent.
- Austria set a new temperature record of 41.2 deg C in early August, breaking the previous high of 41 deg C recorded just a day earlier in Vienna.
AI generated
Vienna – Austria saw its highest-ever recorded number of heat-related deaths this June and July, the country’s health agency said on Aug 30, as Europe reels from a summer of brutal heatwaves.
The AGES agency said those two months saw 646 heat-related deaths, as compared to the previous high of 570 in June and July 2024.
The figures are calculated using a statistical model analysing excess mortality.
Scientific experts say that human-made climate change has made extreme weather events more intense and more frequent, and Europe has become the globe’s fastest-warming continent.
Austria, like much of the rest of the continent, has seen records tumble in this summer’s heatwaves and drought.
A new temperature record of 41.2 deg C was set at Bad Deutsch-Altenburg in eastern Austria in early August, beating a previous high of 41 deg C recorded in Vienna just a day earlier. AFP

items.body_text:
Israeli strike kills two people including a 3-year-old boy, Gaza medics say
CAIRO, Aug 30 - An Israeli airstrike killed two Palestinians, including a three-year-old child, in the central Gaza Strip on Sunday, health officials said.
Gaza medics said the Israeli airstrike near a bakery in Deir Al-Balah killed one man, Hussam Nusair, a three-year-old boy, Tayyem Hamdan, and wounded several others.
The Israeli military said it attacked a Hamas militant, without giving further details.
An October 2025 U.S.-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory, but it failed to end strikes by the Israeli military, which it said aimed to thwart attacks by Hamas and other Gaza militants.
Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement a broader plan by U.S. President Donald Trump to end the Gaza conflict, which also includes Israeli withdrawals and Hamas disarmament.
More than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect last October, according to Gazan health officials, while the Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed. REUTERS

items.body_text:
- 
            Cabinet to support drone bill: sourceNATIONAL DEFENSE: The Executive Yuan refrained from harsh criticism after the opposition backed uncrewed vehicle bill passed, as it plans to co-sign it, sources said
  - By Chung Li-hua / Staff reporter
 The premier is to countersign a Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT)-led bill on defense self-reliance and the uncrewed vehicle industry, and include funding for it in this year’s supplemental budget, sources said yesterday. The Legislative Yuan on Thursday passed the Act on Strengthening Defense Autonomy and Developing the Unmanned Vehicles Industry (強化國防自主暨無人載具產業發展條例), providing for NT$240 billion (US$7.59 billion) over six years in principle, while allowing additional funding subject to legislative approval. The act directs the Ministry of National Defense to prioritize the procurement of domestically produced “low-cost, high-performance” uncrewed systems. It requires the central government to, in principle, earmark NT$40 billion annually for six consecutive years, using its general budget to procure uncrewed vehicles, to reinforce national defense and drive industrial growth. A soldier from the Army Special Operations Command operates drone equipment in an undated photo.Photo courtesy of the Military News Agency The Cabinet’s proposal, which requested NT$210 billion in a special budget over six years, failed to win approval. The bill, backed by the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) caucus, was rejected by the KMT and the smaller opposition Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), which together hold a legislative majority. The legislature only passed this year’s central government budget on Aug. 14. The Cabinet had originally planned to approve the supplemental budget on Thursday, but decided to delay the move by a week, because the legislature was scheduled to vote on the uncrewed vehicle bill that day, sources said. The Cabinet also planned to adjust the supplemental budget depending on the outcome of the vote, they said. The Executive Yuan wants to accelerate defense buildup and is preparing to co-sign the uncrewed vehicle bill, they said, adding that therefore, following the passage of the opposition-led version on Thursday, it refrained from harsh criticism and instead expressed deep regret and said it would “expedite the allocation of the necessary funding.” The ministry has confirmed that all items cut from the Cabinet’s NT$1.25 trillion defense special bill would be included in this year’s supplemental budget, which means funding for uncrewed vehicles would also be included, the source said. Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) is expected to make the final decision on the amount of the supplemental budget after receiving a report from the ministry this week, sources said. The Cabinet initially planned to fund uncrewed vehicles through a special budget, so no funding for the program was included in next year’s central government budget. As the budget proposal must be submitted to the legislature tomorrow, there is not enough time to revise it beforehand, sources said. Waiting until next year’s budget is passed before seeking additional funding could be too slow, they said. The Executive Yuan is expected to submit amendments to the budget at an appropriate time, so it can be reviewed alongside the main budget proposal by the legislature, they said.  The US backed Taiwan’s continued participation in the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) as Taiwan and associated countries sent senior delegations to the summit this week. The 55th PIF Leaders Meeting is being held from today to Friday in Koror, Palau, with presidents and high-level officials from Pacific nations including the Marshall Islands, Tuvalu, New Zealand, Australia and Fiji expected to attend. items.title: Low-pressure system to bring unstable weather
items.body_text:
- 
            Low-pressure system to bring unstable weather
  - Staff writer, with CNA
 Taiwan is forecast to have unstable weather this week, with a low-pressure system expected to bring heavy rain to some areas, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday. Moisture carried by southwesterly winds, combined with the low-pressure system, is expected to affect central and southern Taiwan this week, with intermittent rain possible throughout the day and heavy localized rainfall forecast in southern areas, the CWA said. Elsewhere, active convection is expected to bring afternoon showers during the week, it added. A graphic shows expected rainfall around Taiwan from today until Saturday.Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration The low-pressure system could lead to the development of more tropical weather systems, creating uncertainty about the weather, it said. The low-pressure system began impacting Taiwan yesterday, it said. A heavy rain advisory was issued in 15 administrative regions across the country yesterday. A heavy rain warning means rainfall of more than 80mm in 24 hours or more than 40mm in one hour, according to the CWA. Today, brief localized showers are expected in southern and eastern Taiwan, while partly cloudy to sunny skies are forecast elsewhere and afternoon showers are possible in mountainous areas south of Hsinchu County, the CWA said. From tomorrow through Wednesday, northern, eastern and southern Taiwan should see brief showers, while heavy rain is possible in mountainous areas of central and southeastern Taiwan in the afternoons, it said. On Thursday and Friday, sporadic rainfall is likely in Keelung, along the northern coast, and in southern and eastern Taiwan, with mostly cloudy skies forecast elsewhere and afternoon thunderstorms possible, it added. WeatherRisk, a Taiwanese weather forecasting page, said that a low-pressure disturbance is expected to move near Taiwan from Wednesday through Friday. It remains unclear whether the system would strengthen into a tropical depression or typhoon, but it is expected to bring more unstable weather, with rain across Taiwan and a chance of heavy downpours, it said in a post. Projections for the system’s intensity and track remain highly uncertain, it said, urging the public to keep an eye on the latest forecasts this week.

Latest figures from both countries put the number of missing at 3,044 , with […]
items.body_text:
Rescuers in Nepal and China battled Sunday through leg-sucking mud and the threat of rising rivers and a newly formed lake to search for thousands missing after a deadly wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayas, engulfing entire villages.
Latest figures from both countries put the number of missing at 3,044 , with a further 750 confirmed deaths — and reports of some bodies possibly swept downstream as far away as India.
The disaster, which struck the China-Nepal border Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse, sending a wall of water and debris downstream, the US Geological Survey said.
Chinese rescuers near the Tibet border port that was hit by a deadly mudslide were “moved to a safe location” Sunday, after a new lake was formed by a landslide, state media reported.
Nepali army troops and engineers were working on Sunday to rescue workers believed trapped in a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site after they successfully inserted a pipe into the passage.
They have “started sending air through the small opening”, Nepali Home Minister Sudan Gurung said in a statement.
Overnight rain and rising river waters hampered efforts early Sunday, filling the excavation area with water before conditions eased and teams resumed efforts, the Nepal army said.
In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority listed 933 hydropower workers among the missing.
China’s state news agency Xinhua reported on Sunday that experts had said “a glacier on the southern slope of Lirung Peak in Nepal” fractured, triggering an ice-rock avalanche.
It said the torrent plummeted rapidly, forming a massive debris flow that travelled more than 20 kilometres before crashing into Gyirong Port.
“The sudden glacial collapse and flash flood is a devastating reminder of how fragile these mountain environments can be,” UN climate chief Simon Steill said in a statement.
‘Nothing left’
Survivors face an agonising wait to learn the fate of missing relatives and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away,” Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.
“There is nothing left.”
At an army base serving as a rescue hub in Bidur, relatives crowded around lists of rescued people pasted on a wall.
“I have come here looking for my son,” said Kalka Sharda, scanning the list in desperation.
On Sunday Nepal’s disaster authority said 589 foreigners, including trekkers and Hindu pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, were unaccounted for.
The Isha Foundation, led by Indian guru Sadhguru, said in an Instagram post on Saturday that 80 members had been on a group trip in the area.
“At this time, there seems to be no encouraging indications of survivors at the immigration office area,” the post said.
‘Enormous’ trauma
The United States and Canada said they would provide $3.6 million each in humanitarian aid to Nepal.
The UK has offered $6.8 million, while the UN released $2.5 million in emergency funding.
The European Union on Friday promised $2.3 milllion, while the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it had allocated more than $1 million and launched an emergency appeal for $31 million.
Nepal’s economy is already under pressure, with limited resources to respond to a disaster of this scale and Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal saying the reconstruction bill could run into “billions of dollars”.
He appealed for specialised assistance, including heavy-lift drones and technology to help locate people who are trapped.
Malaysia said it would send search and rescue specialists to assist and would also contribute US$1 million to Nepal to help the recovery efforts and victims.
Khanal also called for forensic testing kits to identify bodies and freezer units to store them, saying bodies that have been in water could decompose at a faster rate.

items.summary: Chinese officials tightened the rules for selling unfinished homes on Friday as they try to lift the country’s property market out of a years-long slump that has weighed on consumption. Half-built apartment buildings dot cities across China, relics of a property boom that came to a halt when the government clamped down on excessive borrowing […]
items.body_text:
China tightens rules on selling unfinished homes to lift sector
Chinese officials instructed local authorities on Friday to “vigorously and orderly promote the sale of ready-to-move-in commercial housing”, while they also urged more protections for buyers who purchase homes before construction is complete.
Chinese officials tightened the rules for selling unfinished homes on Friday as they try to lift the country’s property market out of a years-long slump that has weighed on consumption.
Half-built apartment buildings dot cities across China, relics of a property boom that came to a halt when the government clamped down on excessive borrowing and rampant speculation in 2020.
That left several developers grappling with massive debt — wreaking havoc on buyers who poured their savings into new homes that were never finished.
Chinese officials instructed local authorities on Friday to “vigorously and orderly promote the sale of ready-to-move-in commercial housing”, while they also urged more protections for buyers who purchase homes before construction is complete.
The instructions came in a joint statement from China’s National Financial Regulatory Administration, as well as Beijing’s housing and natural resource ministries.
The financial regulator and China’s central bank also announced on Friday new lending guidelines that raise the maximum length for personal housing loans to 40 years, from the existing 30-year mortgage limit.
“These policies are a meaningful step in the right direction,” wrote Zhiwei Zhang, President and Chief Economist at Pinpoint Asset Management.
“The decision to allow mortgage loans up to 40 years helps to mitigate the home buyers’ debt burden,” he said.
China’s leaders have battled sluggish domestic spending since the end of the Covid-19 pandemic, which has threatened growth even as exports and certain high-tech sectors boom.
“The weak domestic demand is to a large extent due to the troubled property sector,” Zhang said, adding that the new housing policies showed officials “understand the urgency” to stabilise the market.

The number of missing soared close to 3,000 Saturday, latest figures from both countries showed, with 633 bodies recovered — and reports of […]
items.body_text:
Rescuers in Nepal and China were still battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing villages.
The number of missing soared close to 3,000 Saturday, latest figures from both countries showed, with 633 bodies recovered — and reports of some dead possibly swept downstream as far away as India.
In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list already including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.
Those that made it out say they have lost everything and now face an agonising wait to discover the fate of missing loved ones, and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away. There is nothing left,” survivor Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP.
Samjhana Thing said she had been waiting three days for news of her missing brother.
“We don’t know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place,” she said.
‘Enormous’ trauma
The trauma of Wednesday’s catastrophe has been “enormous”, and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected, the Red Cross said, with the death toll expected to rise.
Emergency teams had been racing to retrieve survivors from affected zones, where the widespread devastation meant food and water supplies were running out.
Compounding the search for the missing have been fears of further flooding in affected areas.
The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes to form, and one of these formations has become a direct threat to emergency workers scouring the region for survivors.
Nepali police urged all rescuers to “immediately move to a safe location”, saying they had received information that “a water dam has burst again on the Tibetan side”.
In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, Beijing suspended its rescue operation at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding, before saying the threat had eased.
State news agency Xinhua reported early Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the area.
‘All swept away’
On the Nepali side of the border, the military located people trapped in the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to extract the survivors.
“Two helicopters have been dispatched, but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
Some 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, he added, but efforts were ongoing to rescue more than a hundred trapped in the same area.
Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
Buddha Tamang told AFP he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck.
“The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away,” Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours, told AFP.
Nepal reported a death toll of 626 people on Saturday.
There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in Nepal.
Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists — seven people died and 554 remain missing, the state Xinhua news agency reported early Saturday.
Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.
In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.
Pilgrimage route
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.
Sivaranjani Muthunathan was travelling by bus with 56 others towards the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam.

items.body_text:
Advertisement
Opinion
Will US threats over Iran be the last straw for Beijing?
China’s measured stance since the Xi-Trump summit in May is reaching a tipping point as US pressure mounts
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva. 
Earlier this month, when US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened sanctions against any nation continuing to purchase Iranian crude oil, he did not name China. He did not need to. China, the Islamic Republic’s largest oil customer, is squarely in Washington’s crosshairs.
The US has already unveiled new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels linked to Iranian trade, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong. Just three months after the May summit between President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump appeared to stabilise bilateral trade relations, the fragile calm is being tested again.
So far, China has signalled it will not be coerced. The stand-off sets the stage for what could be the next major rupture in an already fraught relationship.
Washington has not been idle since May. In June, the Pentagon added dozens of companies – including Alibaba, Baidu and BYD – to its list of “Chinese military companies”, a designation that can restrict these companies’ access to US capital and market. In July, it announced a 10-12.5 per cent tariff on goods from 60 economies, including China, following its Section 301 investigation into forced labour.
This was followed by a ban on imports of Chinese robots and power inverters (July) and a 15 per cent tariff on polysilicon (August). The cumulative message is clear: Washington is tightening the screws on multiple fronts, and Iran is merely the latest lever.
Beijing’s response to this onslaught has been deliberate and calibrated. Gone are the days of blanket tariff retaliation. Instead, China has preferred to hold its fire where the cost of escalation outweighs the benefits, striking back with precision when core interests are threatened.

Arthritis drug restores 100% of hair on some patients with severe alopecia in global trial
Tests at hospitals in the US, Europe and China discover medication can help to reverse hair loss caused by the autoimmune disease
The condition is called alopecia areata. It is an autoimmune disease where the body’s own immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, causing unpredictable hair loss. Sometimes it is just a few patches but in severe cases, the entire scalp, eyebrows and even body hair can vanish. Until now, there has been no reliably effective treatment.
Enter upadacitinib. This once-daily oral medication was previously approved to tame inflammation in various forms of arthritis. But scientists suspected it might also help with alopecia areata by calming the same kind of immune overreaction that destroys hair follicles.
On average, the volunteers had lost about 84 per cent of their scalp hair. Some had not seen any regrowth for at least six months.
Participants were randomly assigned to take either a 15mg dose, a 30mg dose, or a placebo pill every day. The results, published in JAMA Dermatology on August 12, were striking.
Within just 24 weeks, roughly half of those taking upadacitinib – both doses combined – saw at least 80 per cent of their scalp hair grow back.

items.body_text:
首場「競來坐坐」開講 莊競程：新竹新製程打造幸福科技城
竹市首場「競來坐坐」古賢開講，莊競程提「幸福新製程」要打造幸福科技城。（民進黨竹市黨部提供）
民進黨新竹市長參選人莊競程今晚在古賢里集會所舉辦首場地方政見說明會「競來坐坐」，與在地鄉親面對面交流。莊競程表示，未來將以「幸福新製程」為城市治理方向，從長輩照顧、交通、教育到城市建設，一項一項解決市民生活中的問題，讓科技發展真正轉化為生活品質，打造新竹成為「幸福科技城」。
莊競程表示，新竹是台灣的鑽石，這座小而美的城市，不只有全球知名的竹科、2所國立頂尖大學，也有超過300年歷史的文化底蘊。市民期待城市持續進步，讓科技發展不只反映在產值上，也能實質提升生活品質。
莊競程說，過去的醫學工程背景，讓他特別重視長輩福利。他提出老人福利三項方向，包括65歲以上市民健保費由市府補助、推動50歲以上市民第一劑帶狀疱疹疫苗免費施打，同時推動敬老愛心卡加碼到1200點、點數可跨月累積並擴大使用範圍，讓長輩照顧更有感，也減輕家庭負擔。
針對南寮建設，莊競程表示，未來若擔任市長，將積極推動設立南寮運動中心，讓市民就近運動、親子家庭有更便利的休閒空間。交通方面也會全力推動捷運開工，並主張捷運綠線應從市區延伸到南寮，串連市中心與海濱觀光帶，改善通勤品質，也帶動南寮的觀光、人潮與商機。
莊競程強調，「競來坐坐」就是希望用最貼近市民的方式，坐下來一起吃頓飯、聊聊新竹的大小事。首場從古賢里出發，未來也將持續走進各里、各社區，傾聽不同世代、不同職業、不同家庭的需求。他說，市長的責任不只是提出願景，更要把市民每天遇到的問題一項一項解決，並為下一個10年、20年的新竹預先規劃，打下堅實基礎。
莊競程指出，未來的新竹，應該是一座讓年輕人看得見希望、長輩生活有尊嚴、家庭育兒更安心的城市。他承諾，未來一定會以專業、效率與溫度推動市政，讓新竹從「科技之都」進一步成為「幸福科技城」。

items.body_text:
吉力吉撈鞏冠盜壘成功。（記者林正堃攝）
〔記者羅志朋／台北報導〕味全龍隊長吉力吉撈．鞏冠單場敲2安、跑回2分，助隊以3：0擊敗台鋼雄鷹，值得一提的是，2局下吉力吉撈敲安，接著靠暴投上二壘，再罕見成功盜上三壘，引起現場球迷一陣驚呼，朱育賢適時安打送回隊長先馳得點。
今天賽後味全總教練葉君璋笑說，「（看到吉力吉撈盜三壘）有一點嚇到，感覺他腳也不是真的那麼慢，哈哈，那是他自己要跑的，可能要證明自己很能跑，然後不要換代跑，哈哈。」葉總受訪時不斷發出招牌笑聲，場面相當歡樂。
吉力吉撈成功盜上三壘並非生涯首例，葉總說，之前擔心吉力吉撈的腳部，這次看他盜三壘有一點嚇到，「我以為是劉俊緯。」
吉力吉撈透露，當時一出局，感覺先發投手江承諺沒有注意他，似乎還在深呼吸，剛好輪到左打朱育賢打擊，三壘手黃劼希離壘包滿遠的，覺得好像有機會就大膽地跑，「有時候投手不會那麼注意我，在場上觀察守備陣型，如果時機抓得好就有機會盜壘成功。」
這是本季吉力吉撈首盜，他說，「我想說本季首盜什麼時候會出現，之前膝蓋受傷不太敢跑，今天沒穿護膝就跑，順便測試一下。」
吉力吉撈中職生涯發動8次盜壘只失敗1次，盜壘成功率超高，他笑說，「是嗎？吳東融跟我說，如果你要跑的話就要safe，不然的話就不要跑，如果之後愈跑愈多，投手應該就會牽制了，一年不會跑太多啦！」

items.body_text:
與帛琉總統試乘MIT電動巴士 林佳龍：台帛攜手前進願景不變
在「政府聯合辦公大樓」（One Stop Shop）太陽能及儲能計畫方面，已安裝600瓩太陽能板及2兆瓦的儲能電池，將帛琉政府聯合辦公大樓打造為綠色建築。（圖擷取自林佳龍臉書）
外交部長林佳龍率團訪問友邦帛琉，今日與帛琉總統惠恕仁（Surangel S. Whipps, Jr.）一同見證帛琉氫能倡議啟動，並試乘今日交車的MIT（台灣製）電動巴士。林佳龍表示，台帛長期維持堅定友好夥伴關係，攜手前進願景不變。
外交部長林佳龍今日出席氫能倡議啟動儀式、聯合辦公大樓太陽能板綠能示範區及電動巴士啟用典禮時致詞表示，台灣與帛琉長期維持堅定而友好的外交夥伴關係，攜手前進的願景始終不變，「Taiwan can help, and Palau can lead」。
林佳龍指出，今日是榮邦計畫架構下台帛具體雙邊合作的又一個重要里程碑。「台帛氫能倡議」是邁向能源自主，以及實現帛琉2032年100%再生能源目標的重要一步，是兩國共同努力的成果，也為更綠色的未來開啟大門。
林佳龍表示，在「政府聯合辦公大樓」（One Stop Shop）太陽能及儲能計畫方面，已安裝600瓩太陽能板及2兆瓦的儲能電池，將帛琉政府聯合辦公大樓打造為綠色建築。這些潔淨能源不僅能供應建築本身使用，也能為電動公車車隊充電。這套完整整合的再生能源系統，結合能源發電、儲存與大眾運輸，為再生能源計畫提供完整的解決方案。
林佳龍今日也與惠恕仁一起試乘甫正式交車的4輛MIT電動巴士。林佳龍說，第55屆太平洋島國論壇（PIF）峰會明日開幕，這批電動公車會協助接送來自整個太平洋地區、遠道而來參加論壇的各國領袖及代表。台帛共同推動的計畫也充分體現今年PIF峰會主題「打造經濟守護生命與提升生活、付諸行動、凝聚團結、生活、行動、團結」，透過建置潔淨能源基礎設施，不僅帶動經濟發展，也改善人民的生活。
林佳龍說，展望未來，太陽能發電系統與電動公車將協助帛琉實現2032年百分之百再生能源的目標，而「台帛氫能倡議」也一定能為區域各國帶來啟發，共同推動永續發展。
林佳龍也透過臉書轉述，惠恕仁今日再次感謝台灣長期在教育、醫療、安全、氣候行動、基礎建設等領域與帛琉並肩合作，並指出，這些計畫帶來的遠超過電力本身，更能提升帛琉的能源自主、保護環境，也為人民帶來更多發展機會。

items.title: As won crashes, rural North Koreans rush to buy dollars
items.summary: A growing number of people in rural North Korea are converting their spare cash into U.S. dollars or Chinese yuan, as fears grow that the North Korean won is rapidly losing value, Daily NK has learned. Even in farming communities that once showed little interest in foreign currency, the belief that holding onto North Korean […]
items.body_text:
A growing number of people in rural North Korea are converting their spare cash into U.S. dollars or Chinese yuan, as fears grow that the North Korean won is rapidly losing value, Daily NK has learned. Even in farming communities that once showed little interest in foreign currency, the belief that holding onto North Korean won “means taking a loss” is spreading.
According to a Daily NK source in North Pyongan province on Wednesday, people in rural areas such as Ryongchon and Tongchang counties have increasingly been traveling to nearby cities to exchange even small amounts of North Korean won for dollars or yuan. Even when the sum is small, people believe holding foreign currency, rather than the domestic won, better protects the value of their savings.
In the past, farming communities had little occasion to use foreign currency in everyday transactions, making them relatively insensitive to exchange rate swings compared with city dwellers. This was especially true in mountainous areas, where jangmadang, the informal markets that have become the backbone of North Korea’s economy since the 1990s, open only about once every ten days, and trade largely takes the form of barter or won transactions, leaving little chance to encounter foreign currency at all.
That began to change in the second half of 2024, when market prices and exchange rates started climbing sharply. Even in rural areas, sellers have increasingly begun pricing goods in won based on that day’s exchange rate. As prices have failed to come down, farming communities have grown more anxious that holding onto won means watching the value of their assets erode.
“The exchange rate has kept rising for the past two years, while the value of the national currency (North Korean won) keeps falling,” the source said. “Even people in rural areas who used to have no interest in foreign currency now feel a strong need to convert even small amounts of money into it.”
The source continued, “Before COVID-19, $100 was worth about 800,000 to 900,000 North Korean won, but now it’s worth about 6 million won. Someone who had 900,000 won back then would only have the equivalent of about $15 today, while someone who had $100 now has 6 million won. That says it all.”
Won described as “worse than paper”
A source in Ryanggang province offered a similar account. “People in border areas use a lot of yuan, but in farming communities where trading isn’t the main livelihood, people tended to hold what little money they had in won,” the source said. “Over the past two years, though, prices and the exchange rate have risen enough to make people’s jaws drop, and it has become the topic of conversation everywhere. That’s made rural people feel it’s urgent to hold yuan too.”
Some in these communities have reportedly gone so far as to say the won “is now worth less than scrap paper” and that “only people who haven’t caught on still hold” it.
“Trust in the national currency was already low because of the currency reform (a reference to North Korea’s 2009 currency redenomination, which wiped out much of the population’s private savings), and it’s been shaken again by the recent surge in prices and the exchange rate,” the source said. “During the currency reform, everyone suffered losses equally. But now the gap between people widens sharply depending on whether they hold foreign currency, and that’s made the preference for it even more pronounced.”
The source added, “No matter how strictly the state cracks down on the use of foreign currency, what’s the point of a crackdown when the value of the national currency keeps falling like this? The reality now is that the belief that holding foreign currency, rather than won, is the only way to avoid losses is only getting stronger.”

items.summary: Heavy rain in Sinuiju has disrupted cross-border cargo truck traffic between North Korea and China, further cooling Chinese investment sentiment that had been building around the anticipated opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, a China-funded crossing linking Sinuiju and Dandong that has stood largely unused since its completion in 2014. Cargo trucks traveling between […]
items.body_text:
Heavy rain in Sinuiju has disrupted cross-border cargo truck traffic between North Korea and China, further cooling Chinese investment sentiment that had been building around the anticipated opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, a China-funded crossing linking Sinuiju and Dandong that has stood largely unused since its completion in 2014.
Cargo trucks traveling between Dandong in China’s Liaoning province and Sinuiju in North Korea’s North Pyongan province stopped running for more than two days starting Aug. 24, a source in North Korea told Daily NK on Friday.
“Trucks that had entered North Korea before Aug. 24 could not return to China, and new trucks could not enter either,” the source said. “There is talk that the cause was a problem in Sinuiju with processing, transporting or storing cargo.”
The exact cause of the suspension has not been officially confirmed, but Chinese trading circles believe it is likely directly linked to recent flooding in Sinuiju caused by heavy rain.
Daily NK previously reported that heavy rain in Sinuiju overwhelmed the city’s weak drainage system, flooding low-lying areas and cutting off electricity and water supplies in some neighborhoods.
Local observers say the low-lying Apkang and Yokjon neighborhoods, which sit near the North Korea-China trade route, may also have seen roads and buildings flooded. Trade and vehicle traffic were likely halted temporarily to prevent further damage during the unloading, storage and transport of cargo, according to the assessment.
Investment mood turns cold
Notably, the incident is also weighing on investment sentiment toward Sinuiju, which had been rising in recent months.
“Businesspeople already knew Sinuiju was geographically vulnerable to flooding, but repeated flood damage like this inevitably changes their thinking,” the source said. “Just as things seemed to be going well, the uncontrollable variable of natural disaster resurfaced and threw cold water on the investment mood.”
The source added, “Many people had shown interest in the idea of developing the surrounding area into an international economic zone once the New Yalu River Bridge opens. But after this incident, there is a growing sense that there are problems that need to be resolved before questions like when the bridge will open or where to invest.”
Among Chinese businesspeople, a growing view holds that simply signing contracts with North Korea and building factories or warehouses is not enough to guarantee stability, and that North Korea must first upgrade its infrastructure to withstand flooding.
“There is growing concern that without protective construction work, such as raising the ground level with soil or rock fill and installing proper waterproofing and drainage systems, a single heavy rain could cause serious damage,” the source said. “Businesspeople have also grown more alert to natural disasters after seeing a string of sudden flood damage in border regions, including recent flooding in Nepal.”
The repeated flooding in Sinuiju is once again highlighting the city’s geographic limitations and weak infrastructure. As flood risk emerges as a major variable for Chinese businesspeople who had shown interest in investing in North Korea, attention is turning to what impact this will have on development around the New Yalu River Bridge, an area that had drawn attention amid expanding North Korea-China customs trade.
Reporting from inside North Korea
Daily NK operates networks of sources inside North Korea who document events in real-time and transmit information through secure channels. Unlike reporting based on state media, satellite imagery, or defector accounts from years past, our journalism comes directly from people currently living under the regime. We verify reports through multiple independent sources and cross-reference details before publication.
Our sources remain anonymous because contact with foreign media is treated as a capital offense in North Korea — discovery means imprisonmen

items.title: North Korea’s Sinuiju underwater again as drainage system fails
items.summary: Sinuiju, the North Pyongan province city that suffered catastrophic flood damage in the summer of 2024, is underwater again, this time because a short burst of intense rain overwhelmed the city’s weak drainage system rather than the Yalu River overflowing its banks. With low-lying neighborhoods submerged and power and water cut off, the flooding has […]
items.body_text:
Sinuiju, the North Pyongan province city that suffered catastrophic flood damage in the summer of 2024, is underwater again, this time because a short burst of intense rain overwhelmed the city’s weak drainage system rather than the Yalu River overflowing its banks. With low-lying neighborhoods submerged and power and water cut off, the flooding has become the latest sign of how fragile North Korea’s urban infrastructure remains against extreme weather.
According to a Daily NK source in North Pyongan province who spoke Thursday, heavy rain pounded the Sinuiju area on Aug. 23 and 24. The downpour briefly let up on Aug. 25 before picking up again overnight into Aug. 26.
“During the flooding in 2024, the river overflowed and that caused the damage. This time, the damage happened because the rainwater couldn’t drain away,” the source said. “The standing water can’t recede, and since it keeps raining, there’s even less chance for it to drain, so many areas remain flooded.”
“The rain stopped briefly on Aug. 25, and we thought the water might start receding, but it began raining again overnight into the early hours of Aug. 26,” the source added. “With the rain continuing like this, people don’t know when the water will finally recede, and they’re feeling anxious.”
The pattern of this flooding is markedly different from the 2024 disaster, according to the source. In 2024, the Yalu River overflowed and heavily damaged Wihwa Island and areas along the riverbank. This time, weak drainage conditions caused flooding across low-lying areas throughout the city.
In Sumun neighborhood, both electricity and water service remained cut off as of Aug. 26, and a significant number of single-story homes were submerged, forcing people to evacuate to higher ground. Temporary shelters have also been set up in some neighborhoods, including Ryonsang and Ryonha, to house flood victims as part of the response, according to the source.
Little state aid expected this time
Amid the damage, flood victims are reportedly resigned to the idea that nationwide recovery assistance will not follow this time, meaning they will have to rebuild their homes and belongings on their own once the water recedes.
“During the previous flooding, the Yalu River overflowed and the damage was highly visible from the outside, and the Marshal (Kim Jong Un) personally visited the area, so nationwide recovery assistance followed. This time, though, the visible damage isn’t as extensive,” the source said. “So there’s a strong sense among people that they shouldn’t expect much state support and will need to rebuild on their own.”
“In terms of the actual damage people have suffered, this time isn’t much different from before,” the source added. “With electricity and water cut off and homes and belongings submerged for days, people are struggling not only with immediate concerns like food and shelter, but even more with the uncertainty of how they’ll rebuild their lives once the water finally recedes.”
The latest flooding is seen as a case that exposes both the topographical characteristics of the Sinuiju area and its vulnerable drainage infrastructure. With North Korean authorities not disclosing detailed information about the damage this time, attention is turning to how extensive and thorough any future recovery efforts will be.
Rodong Sinmun reported Aug. 26 that rain and showers fell across most of the country between Aug. 23 and 24 due to a low-pressure trough and the seasonal rain front, with heavy rain also reported in several areas of North Pyongan province, some areas of South Pyongan province, and localized areas of Jagang province.
According to the newspaper, on Aug. 24 alone, Kusong received 408 millimeters of rain, Sinuiju 379 millimeters, Chonma 365 millimeters, Wihwa Island 329 millimeters, Uiju and Taechon 319 millimeters, Phihyon 267 millimeters, Nyongbyon 224 millimeters and Taegwan 216 millimeters, all considered extremely heavy rainfall. items.title: 'I was a wreck': Popyrin bares his soul before US Open bid
items.summary: One-time Novak Djokovic slayer Alexei Popyrin turns to Oscar Piastri's esteemed mindset coach in the hope of rediscovering the giddy heights of tennis.
items.body_text:
In short:
Australia's Alexei Popyrin is working with F1 driver Oscar Piastri's mindset coach Emma Murray as he prepares for his latest US Open campaign.
Popyrin slipped as far as number 139 in the rankings, but has received a wildcard to this year's tournament.
What's next?
Popyrin will play former US Open semi-finalist Grigor Dimitrov in round one at Flushing Meadows.
Alexei Popyrin hit rock bottom when he feared he wouldn't enjoy even his own wedding next month.
From the giddy high of taking down Novak Djokovic at the 2024 US Open, Popyrin needed a wildcard into this year's New York grand slam after slumping to as low as number 139 in the rankings last month.
He knew then he needed professional help.
The fallen Australian tennis star turned to Oscar Piastri's esteemed mindset coach and credits Emma Murray for helping him find contentment again. To a point.
"It's not easy," Popyrin said in a raw interview ahead of his first-round Open date with former semi-finalist turned 2026 qualifier Grigor Dimitrov.
"A lot of that is what was eating at me, thinking about things, searching for that feeling of being at the career-high rankings, of playing at that level, and it becomes a kind of an unhealthy obsession.
"It becomes a really negative and bad balance between you and tennis and it's what was really not helping me and it was the main culprit in what has been happening over the last few months.
"I needed to change that and I needed to change just the whole way I look at tennis as a whole, and it's still a work in progress and it's not going to be a quick fix over one or two weeks."
Popyrin took his first mental-health break after Wimbledon last year before needing another reset following a straight-sets first-round loss at the All England Club six weeks ago to Jiri Lehecka.
"After Wimbledon, I was a wreck," said the former French Open junior champion.
"I used to — well, I still do — every time I lose, I think I don't deserve to have fun. After, I think I don't deserve to be happy.
"I was worried that I wouldn't enjoy my wedding because of my tennis, and when I had that thought for the first time I was like, 'OK, something is really, really wrong and I've really got to take some time and figure things out.'"
The 27-year-old one-time world number 19 has been working with Murray for only a short time, but already the high-performance emotional regulator is making progress.
"I'm trying to not associate my results with how I feel as a person," Popyrin said.
"I'm trying to look at it in a way that it's just a journey that I'm on. Where I am is where I am and what I have to do is just continue trusting the process that I'm on.
"I've stuck with the same team and I haven't changed anything. I believe in the guys. I believe in myself. I believe that everything is just mental for me.
"And if I'm able to make those changes up in my head, then I'm able to not only get to where I am, but I believe I can go further.
"I've got to kind of start from scratch, which is never easy. It's something I have done before, but it's even harder for me to do that because of where I have been and what I have done and what I have achieved.
"But it's important for me if I want to continue playing tennis that I get through this, and the way I get through this is continuing on the trajectory that I have been the last month."
AAP

items.title: Dees deliver Lions' greatest AFLW defeat, Port star's cruel injury blow
items.summary: Melbourne steams past Brisbane to claim a 3-0 start to the season; while Port Adelaide loses Indy Tahau to a suspected knee injury, overshadowing a win over GWS.
items.body_text:
Melbourne hands Brisbane greatest AFLW loss, Port Adelaide star injured, wins for Hawthorn, Geelong
In short:
Melbourne dominated Brisbane by 56 points to claim a perfect 3-0 start to the season.
Port Adelaide lost star forward Indy Tahau to a suspected knee injury, overshadowing a win over GWS.
Richmond claimed a thrilling five-point win over Essendon in the Dreamtime match in Darwin, while Carlton, Geelong and Hawthorn also enjoyed victories.
Melbourne has steamed past an injury-ravaged Brisbane by 56 points to claim a perfect 3-0 start to the AFLW season.
Elsewhere, Port Adelaide lost star forward Indy Tahau to a suspected serious knee injury, overshadowing a thrilling four-point win over GWS in Canberra, while Richmond, Carlton, Hawthorn and Geelong all claimed victories on a busy day across the league.
Brisbane grabbed the first goal but the Demons were unstoppable from there, kicking the next 12 and going on to hand the Lions their heaviest AFLW defeat, a 14.5 (89) to 4.9 (33) shellacking at Casey Fields.
Liv Purcell (31 disposals) continued her magnificent form along with Tyla Hanks (24 disposals, eight tackles and a goal), while Kate Hore (24) was prolific, and Tahlia Gillard (11 intercepts) led an impressive defence.
Ryleigh Wotherspoon (three goals, eight tackles), Georgia Gall (two), Mia Austin (two) and Megan Fitzsimon (two) hit the scoreboard.
Lions Marlow Graham (concussion) and Neesa Dooley (collarbone) were both hurt in the first quarter.
Then Belle Dawes (right shoulder) and Ruby Svarc (concussion) were worse for wear after colliding with each other.
Dawes played through pain and finished with 24 disposals and a goal, while Orla O'Dwyer (21) was strong.
Sophie Conway (left knee) and Eleanor Hartill (foot) also played through issues.
Tahau, who previously tore her left ACL, was helped off with a right knee injury late in the third quarter of Port Adelaide's 7.10 (52) to 8.0 (48) victory at Manuka Oval.
It was a tight contest all day and Port led by nine at three-quarter time before Brodee Mowbray goaled twice to put GWS in front.
GWS led until the death, when Port's Matilda Scholz took a terrific intercept mark to create a late attack that ended with Lauren Young marking and kicking the winner with seconds left.
Scholz (30 hit-outs, 24 disposals) was dominant, while Piper Window kicked three goals.
Alyce Parker (21 disposals) was busy for GWS (1-2), who shared the goals around.
At Victoria Park, Hawthorn won their second game of the season, with a 28-point victory over Collingwood.
It was a close game in the opening quarter, with the Hawks leading by eight points at the first change.
They then went on with it, however, kicking 6.3 to 2.7 in the final three terms.
A four-goal-to-one third quarter made the difference, with Jasmine Fleming kicking one of the goals of the day with a brilliant right-foot finish from deep in the pocket.
Aine McDonagh, who last week surpassed Cora Staunton as the most prolific AFLW goal-kicker from Ireland with three goals against Port Adelaide, repeated the dose with another three majors against the Pies to take her career haul to 59.
Ruck Lucy Wales had another big game for Hawthorn, with 23 disposals, 22 hit-outs, nine marks, five tackles and four score involvements.
For the Pies, there were no multiple goal-kickers, with majors to Ruby Schleicher, Ash Centra and Dominique Carbone.
A five-goal final quarter from the Suns was not enough, as Gold Coast fell seven points short against Geelong at Carrara.
The Suns led by two points at quarter time, and four at the long break before a three-goal-to-one third term gave Geelong the break.
Gold Coast came home with 5.1, but the Cats kicked 4.1 to hold on to win 10.4 (64) to 8.9 (57).
Charlie Rowbottom had 39 disposals in a losing cause, while Havana Harris kicked three for the Suns - including the final goal of the game on the siren.
Ava Usher and Alannah Welsh both booted two for the home side.
Geelong's Georgie Prespakis had 33 disposals

items.title: Federer tears up during Tennis Hall of Fame induction
items.summary: The emotions flow for tennis legend Roger Federer, who says he is still writing his love letter to the game as he is inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame.
items.body_text:
In short:
Swiss tennis legend Roger Federer says his induction to the International Tennis Hall of Fame was "not a goodbye" to the game he loves.
Federer, the 20-time major champion, was emotional at the ceremony after being introduced by his wife Mirka.
Broadcaster and journalist Mary Carillo was also inducted, introduced by tennis great Billie Jean King.
An emotional Roger Federer said he was still writing his love letter to the sport that "meant the world" to him as the 20-time Grand Slam champion was inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in Newport, Rhode Island.
Federer, who was inducted alongside broadcaster and journalist Mary Carillo, reflected on his storied career in a speech that brought him to tears a few times.
"This is one of the greatest honours of my life," Federer said. "They call this the Hall of Fame, but fame was never the goal.
"My goal was to spend my life doing something I love … with people who love it as much as I do."
His opening words, after his introduction speech from his wife Mirka, were: "Oh man. This is very high level and a tough act to follow."
He joked: "I don't know if you have been practising secretly" before praising his wife's presentation of the 274th Hall of Famer.
It began to get tough for him about halfway through, when he talked about his childhood hero, Stefan Edberg, when he said these are "happy tears."
Then he was brought to tears again when he spoke about his longtime coach Severin Luthi, before he wanted to thank Mirka for helping him on his journey.
"Now the Mirka part," he said, pausing before breaking into tears. "Oh gosh, this such a mess."
He tried to joke, but the tears took over like a quick return at the net.
"I need tissues and sunglasses, everything to protect me right now," he told the crowd, fighting back more tears.
The Swiss captured a men's-record eight Wimbledon titles and spent 310 weeks as the world number one. He also won six Australian Open crowns, five US Open titles and one French Open title.
And he did it all while playing with elegance, a signature headband – apparently wearing more than 5,000 of them during his career, he quipped in his address – and almost always two pairs of socks.
"Tennis meant the world to me. Not just playing, not just winning, but creating something new," said Federer, who retired in 2022 with 103 ATP Tour titles.
"It's a mentality I have. I used to play serve and volley, I had a transition game, I played way beyond the baseline sometimes, or on top of the baseline.
"And I would even try to sneak up on my opponents on my return, and some call it the SABR [Sneak Attack by Roger] today.
"This is what was important to me on the court, but so much of what was really important happened off the court."
The 45-year-old got emotional while thanking his coaches, doctors and family, including wife Mirka, who praised Federer for his character off the court as husband, father and friend.
As his name entered the Hall of Fame, Federer said he was proud that Switzerland was coming with him, recalling how he loved watching tennis as a 13-year-old ball boy in Basel.
"I'm still writing my love letter to tennis, and my time as a player is done, but tennis will always stand at the intersection of everything I care most about," he said.
"My family, our friendships, the past 40 years, the future we're building – tennis, for me, is responsible for it all. So this is not a goodbye."
The Swiss said he was "incredibly lucky" to have played with different generations of tennis players, from Andre Agassi and Lleyton Hewitt to Andy Roddick, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic.
But he added that his induction was not only an opportunity to look back on his career, but also ahead to the future of the game.
"We all leave the court eventually, but the sport keeps evolving," Federer said.

items.title: Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data
items.summary: A new round of privacy laws designed to protect Australians’ personal information and keep pace with new technology will be unveiled on Monday.
items.body_text:
Privacy laws target AI, smart glasses right to erase Australians’ data
The federal government will unveil a raft of changes to Australia’s privacy laws designed to keep pace with new technologies including smart glasses and artificial intelligence.
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland will on Monday release the draft legislation, which will also include new online safeguards for identity documents, called IDLock, and a right to have personal information destroyed by social media and search companies.
Smart glasses look like normal glasses but can also photograph or film what the user sees, potentially without the consent or knowledge of other people. The Greens are already proposing new laws that would ban the import of the glasses for the next 12 months because of privacy concerns.
The rise of AI, meanwhile, has seen tech companies shovel huge volumes of data into their systems to help “train” their AI models, with little regard for people’s privacy or copyright.
The law changes will include a right to erasure, so people can ask social media and search companies to have their personal information destroyed, rather than it being retained. The right to erasure will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles.
Rowland said Australians deserved to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver’s licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online.
“As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia’s approach must evolve with them. With the launch of IDLock, our government is taking the next step towards a stronger, more robust identity verification framework that expands the focus from responding after identity credentials have been compromised, to enabling Australians to protect themselves before identity crime occurs,” she said.
“Whether their driver licence details have been exposed in a data breach or they are concerned about scams and identity theft, IDLock will give Australians an accessible and simple way to have greater visibility, control and confidence in how their identity documents are used.”
After an initial trial, IDLock will be added to Australians’ myGov accounts in 2027 and will allow people to block, unblock and monitor the use of their ID documents.
It will help people ensure they do not have their ID stolen or misused in scams and other identity crimes, while also allowing them to see whether their data has been subject to a data breach or hacking incident.
IDLock builds on the Credential Protection Register, created in 2022 by the government, which is supposed to stop compromised identity documents from being used to falsely establish an individual’s identity. The register has blocked over 830,000 fraudulent identity verification attempts since it was established.
After the release of the proposed new laws, the government will consult industry and look to introduce the laws into parliament by the end of 2026.

On a sun-soaked Sunday afternoon at Casey Fields, Melbourne finally beat their bogey team.
The Demons clinched their maiden premiership in the 2022 grand final against the Lions, but lost every single encounter to Brisbane in the three years thereafter.
But Melbourne finally revived the rivalry on Sunday in the AFLW’s Sir Doug Nicholls Round, triumphing over a shell-shocked and injury-marred Brisbane by 56 points, thanks to three goals from Ryleigh Wotherspoon and a career-best performance from Tahlia Gillard.
Under the stewardship of new coach Tom Wilson – who took over from veteran Mick Stinear – Melbourne have now won their opening three games.
The Lions, meanwhile, have lost two in a row following last week’s 11-point loss to North Melbourne in the grand final rematch and lost multiple players to injury on Sunday.
Lions coach Craig Starcevich was short and succinct in a post-match press conference after the disappointing result, noting “everything that could have gone wrong today, went wrong”.
The veteran coach compared dealing with his side’s injury list to “plugging holes in a dam”.
“The group’s pretty strong and pretty resilient, so they’ll keep tracking in,” he said. “From that angle, we’re pretty proud of them. They kept going. I think we levelled up in the last quarter, but that’s a small silver lining to an otherwise ordinary day, but they’re built with the right stuff, and they’ll bounce back and be fine in the coming weeks.”
Starcevich cautioned the Lions were only three games into the season and noted his side had a similar start in 2025.
“This time last year, we were in the same boat, 1-2 and we managed to find something and get on a bit of a roll and be there at the end,” he said.
“Nothing’s that predictable going forward, but we’ve been in this situation before, and I’ll back our players to fight their way out of it.”
Melbourne got off to a sluggish start, unable to lock the ball inside their forward 50 until Megan Fitzsimon scored a major after a strong performance from former Blue Mia Austin.
The end of the first quarter was marred by a heavy collision between Georgia Campbell and Brisbane’s Neasa Dooley, which left the Lion lying on the grass in agony, clutching her collarbone.
Escorted by trainers and doctors, Dooley was clapped off the field by concerned spectators. But Brisbane’s injury carnage didn’t end there. Bel Dawes copped some friendly fire and Marlo Graham came off the field due to concussion protocols in a separate incident.
At one point in the second quarter, Brisbane had three players off the ground with injuries being assessed, and another two players who needed to spend time off the ground.
There was a healthy contingent of Brisbane supporters who made the trek from Casey Fields on Sunday. But by half-time, the Lions supporters were silent.
Wotherspoon and Eliza McNamara piled on the pressure with multiple goals, while Brisbane’s usually dependable Dakota Davidson was kept quiet and limited to behinds.
The Lions supporters briefly had something to cheer about when a bunny raced across Casey Field, happily speeding alongside the boundary line and thankfully avoiding getting hit by a Sherrin.
Irishwoman Orla O’Dwyer limited the scoreboard damage in the final quarter, weaving around her opponent to slot a goal before accidentally crashing into the left goalpost.

items.title: ‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death
items.summary: The father of Anthony, Mundine snr was the only Australian boxer to compete professionally across four weight divisions and held four different Australian titles.
items.body_text:
‘Broken’: Anthony Mundine reacts to father and boxing great Tony Mundine’s death
Updated ,first published
Warning: This story contains images and the name of a deceased Indigenous person.
Australian boxing great Tony Mundine has died, age 75.
The boxer, who is also the father of professional boxer and rugby league player Anthony Mundine, died at the weekend, sources close to the family have confirmed to this masthead.
Mundine was the only Australian boxer to compete professionally across four weight divisions and held four different Australian titles.
On Sunday night, Anthony Mundine said he was “broken” in an Instagram post.
“Dad I love you man my Allah bless your soul. I’m on my way home to say goodbye one last time til we meet again... there’s only one Tony Mundine.”
In 2024, Anthony Mundine described his father as his “biggest inspiration” in and out of the ring.
“You’ve shown me what it means to be a man of strength and integrity, and for that, I’m forever grateful. I wouldn’t be who I am without your sacrifices, your wisdom, and your unwavering support,” he wrote at the time.
Tony Mundine retired from professional boxing in 1984 and became a member of the Order of Australia in 1986 for services to sport, particularly boxing and Aboriginal youth.
A Bundjalung man from Baryulgil, just north of the NSW town of Grafton, Mundine moved to Sydney in the mid-1960s with the hope of becoming a first grade footballer.
He played with the Redfern All Blacks and it was while doing some off-season training at a local boxing gym his talent was discovered.
Mundine had his first fight in Sydney in 1969 - competing in 96 bouts in a career that spanned till 1984 that also saw him travel the world and challenge unsuccessfully once for the World Middleweight belt in 1974.
Upon his retirement from boxing, Mundine was heavily involved in a gym in the neighbourhood known as The Block in Redfern, on the corner of Eveleigh and Vine Streets.
The gym had been set up inside an old shoe factory that had been acquired by the Aboriginal Housing Company and Mundine’s work had a positive impact on young Aboriginal people as the venue became a popular place for the community to spend time.

items.body_text:
Several leaders have pulled out of a the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Palau at the eleventh hour.
Solomon Islands prime minister, Matthew Wale, has cancelled his appearance after a no-confidence motion was lodged against him at home by the Solomon Islands home affairs minister, Manasseh Maelanga.
Maelanga accused Wale of “repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance without proper consultation with, or the approval of, cabinet, thereby undermining the principles of collective cabinet responsibility, representative democracy and good governance”, according to the ABC.
Australia has been in negotiations with the Solomons on a security treaty, with the hope that further negotiations could have taken place on the sidelines of the summit.
Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, and his Vanuatu counterpart, Jotham Napat, will also not be attending, with the Samoan leader, La’auli Leuatea Schmidt, another notable absence.
The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has confirmed he will still be attending.
Oliver Nobetau, the Lowy Institute’s Pacific Islands program director, said the pulling out by key leaders “dulls the flame” of the meeting.
“This has been shaping up to be quite a significant PIF … it’s really unfortunate that this is the case,” he told Guardian Australia.
“With the pulling out of this many key prime ministers within the region, it dilutes the potential of what could come out of this leaders’ meeting.”
Nobetau said there were high expectations that this leaders’ meeting could progress pilot projects around Pacific climate resilience, and was important ahead of the Cop31 climate summit in November and a pre-Cop31 summit to be held in Fiji and Tuvalu in October.
He added the leaders not showing up could be read as those nations prioritising bilateral agreements with nations including Australia above region-wide commitments.
“PIF has to demonstrate its usefulness as well. While it is a useful forum for a lot of our Pacific members, maybe the bigger countries feel there are more pressing issues or they can achieve more benefits for their countries by engaging bilaterally or directly with other partners.”
Speaking at Queensland Labor conference on Sunday in Brisbane, Albanese said Australia had a duty to help Pacific nations thrive.
Albanese said allowing Pacific nations to succeed would also benefit Australia.
“The big challenges facing the Pacific require solutions designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific,” he told the
“Australia has a key role to play, as a partner and leader.
“In a time of strategic competition in our region, our engagement in the Pacific Islands Forum and our contributions to the infrastructure, regional security and climate action of the region matter more than ever before.”
The visit follows the prime minister signing a security deal with Fiji, elevating the bilateral relationship to a formal alliance as Australia seeks to curb Chinese influence in the region.
Pacific leaders are set to discuss security and climate concerns during the summit.
Albanese said Australia would also seek to reiterate support for Pacific workers coming to the country.
Debate has recently raged over how the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility Scheme cohort would factor into immigration cuts flagged by various parties.
Representatives of the resurgent One Nation have been pressed to clarify that PALM workers, many of whom provide much-needed labour in regional areas, would not be included in a significant reduction to net overseas migration.
Albanese said the migration discussion had been fuelling division and the Pacific worker scheme would continue because of its critical economic benefit.
“People from the Pacific make an enormous contribution to Australia’s prosperity through their vital work in regional industries like agriculture and meat processing,” he said.

items.body_text:
Clair Spry says her sister would hate the attention. She would want it focused on the Nepali people, who have been displaced or are in need of aid. She would want it to be on the impact of the climate crisis, especially on the world’s most economically vulnerable populations.
“Her focus right now would not be on her; it would be on the families,” Spry said. “So many people, the Nepalese people, that have been horribly displaced and traumatised. She would want the attention on them and how we are going to help them.
“And global warming. This is something the poorest people of the world are affected by. It’s not the New Yorkers, it’s the people who are in these parts of the world. For Renee, that would be heartbreaking.”
Like many of the missing Australians, Renee arrived at Gyirong Port just 10 minutes before the flood struck. The area was one of the hardest hit – images from Chinese rescue teams show the area completely flattened. Huge buildings, power lines, everything – just wiped away.
Renee is a disability support worker who lives on the Sunshine Coast. She has been with her partner, Shaun, an emergency nurse, since they were 15, and they share two daughters in their 20s.
Clair has set up a GoFundMe to get the three of them over to Nepal – Shaun wants to travel to the port to try to find any signs of her. And their daughters, Lily and Ruby, don’t want him to go alone.
“Their first reaction is, we have to go. The practicalities, and what can actually be done in the first few days, it hasn’t been possible [to enter the area], but they still want to go,” she said.
“And if they are able to find her, to bring her home.”
Renee’s family understand how dire the situation is, and how unlikely it is that she, or anyone in that same area, survived. But until they know for certain, they would hold hope, she said.
“Everyone’s very realistic. We know how bad this was and where she was. But until they find her, everyone’s got this little slither of hope that maybe she’s stuck somewhere and can’t get out, or she’s injured.
“I’ve been looking through pictures trying to identify someone or see her. But we understand the reality of this situation.”
Like most Australians, Renee had come to Nepal on a pilgrimage. Spry said her sister was a “deeply spiritual” person who loved to help people.
“She had two degrees, and she chose to do something that was … a completely selfless vocation. Her priority was always other people,” she said.
“Every person she touched, they knew her love and kindness. She would be so uncomfortable with all this.”
The family of Michael Keats, an Australian who had been near the Tibet-Nepal border when flash flooding began, confirmed his death in posts to social media on Sunday. 
 Keats’s wife, Emily Boyd, said on Instagram he had been on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash that had been a “dream for many years”.
“Mike went on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash seeking enlightenment,” Boyd said.
“There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted then to know God, and to merge with the divine.
 ”He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend. He showed up for so many people in so many ways. A heart of pure gold. We love you forever and always.”

Here’s a recap of the day’s top headlines:
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has told party faithful in Queensland that “we owe it to history” to defeat rightwing populism, amid a surge in support for One Nation and rising anti-immigration sentiment.
Pauline Hanson’s rightwing party won the Secret Harbour byelection in Western Australia on Saturday. Federal minister Tanya Plibersek said Labor would “have a good look” at the result but that the poll was largely held on state issues.
Plibersek also told ABC’s Insiders that the federal cabinet had never discussed cutting Australia’s refugee intake, contradicting reports this week.
The government is reviewing the import of smartglasses capable of recording video images, Plibersek says.
Missing Australian woman Cara Severino, who had lost contact with her family after flash flooding in Nepal, was safely located. Her family said they were “beyond relieved and elated”.
Speakers at anti-immigration rallies held across the country have taken credit for the surge in support for One Nation.
Mark Latham and right-wing activists address March for Australia rallies
Mark Latham and right-wing influencer Auspill were among the speakers at the “free speech” March for Australia rallies today.
Benjamin van der Linden, from a group called Make Australia Christian Again, posted footage showing Hugo Lennon, who goes by the name Auspill online, leading a march in Melbourne in chants of “Aussie, Aussie, Aussie”.
Latham, the former federal Labor opposition leader and ex-One Nation New South Wales state leader, was among the headline speakers at the Sydney rally today. He called for the abolition of “all the Chris Minns hate speech laws”.
The crowd booed when Anthony Albanese and Mehreen Faruqi’s names were mentioned, but the jeers were loudest when Minns, the NSW premier, was mentioned. Other Sydney speakers included Libertarian MP John Ruddick, Chris Yates from activist group CitizenGO and former federal Liberal MP Ross Cameron.
According to the March for Australia Facebook page, Brisbane’s rally was be addressed by Barclay McGain, a former young Liberal National party member and now in the conservative political action conference (CPAC); the far-right influencer Andre Mamet, known as Ausmaxx; and Harry Richardson, from the British Australian Community, an organisation for “celebrating the ongoing contributions to Australia by people of British Isles descent”.
Queensland police said about 400 people attended the Brisbane CBD rally where two men were directed to move on after “breaching the peace”, a spokesperson said. They said 50 people attended the city’s counterprotest.
NSW police said they issued three men move-on orders.
March for Australia rallies claim credit for One Nation's rise
Luca Ittimani
Hundreds of people have gathered in capital cities at rallies organised under the banner of anti-immigration March for Australia.
Over 300 people gathered for a “free speech” rally in Belmore Park in the Sydney CBD at midday. More than 70 police officers attended, including riot squad officers and mounted police on horseback. A counter-protest had been scheduled for Hyde Park.
Brian Marlow, founder of nationalist activist group Revive Australia, led the rally. Much of the crowd raised their hands when he asked if they had attended the first March For Australia in August 2025. Bec Freedom, who organised the first March For Australia in 2025, received a round of applause.
Marlow said the marches were responsible for One Nation’s subsequent rise in the polls, with the minor party now claiming close to 30% of primary votes and winning the Secret Harbour byelection in WA yesterday.

items.summary: Rescue crews are on scene after a ferry carrying more than 260 passengers capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday.
items.body_text:
Ferry carrying more than 260 passengers capsizes off northern Cyprus
Rescue crews are on scene
A ferry carrying more than 260 passengers capsized off the coast of northern Cyprus on Sunday, Turkish media reported.
The catamaran-style ferry was travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of ethnically divided Cyprus, to the Turkish port of Tasucu in Mersin province.
There are no reports of casualties so far.
The ferry started taking in water a few kilometres off the coast, the Turkish state-run TRT news channel reported.
Northern Cyprus Transportation Minister Erhan Arikli told TRT that the ship had overturned and that rescue crews were already on the scene.
Several companies run ferries on the busy route between Kyrenia and Tasucu. It is not yet known which company was operating the ferry that capsized.
Video footage from the scene shows people with life-vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel.

items.title: As Germany's far right gains ground, coded symbols are hiding in plain sight
items.summary: As Germany’s far right gains political ground, researchers say some of its supporters are becoming more comfortable signalling their views in public — sometimes without displaying an explicitly political symbol at all.
items.body_text:
As Germany's far right gains ground, coded symbols are hiding in plain sight
Supporters have co-opted everyday brands to signal their beliefs while skirting the law
As Germany's far right gains political ground in some parts of the country, researchers say some supporters are getting more comfortable showing their views in public — albeit sometimes without displaying an explicitly political symbol.
At recent rallies for the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, that coded language was visible on things as ordinary as a pair of sneakers or a T-shirt.
Researchers say logos for brands including New Balance and Lonsdale are increasingly used as dog whistles for nationalist and Nazi symbolism — something that is especially significant in Germany, where the display of Nazi symbols is restricted by law.
"What we noticed in the last couple of years is that frequently at these events, you see a lot of people who have different signs which relate to the extreme right," said Gideon Botsch, head of the Emil Julius Gumbel Research Unit on Antisemitism and Right-Wing Extremism at Potsdam University.
"Some are clear and open right-wing and neo-Nazi symbols ... others are opaque or playing the game a little bit."
Some have co-opted New Balance, taking the large "N" on the side of its sneakers to mean "nationalist" and "NB" for Nationale Bewegung, or "national movement," Botsch said.
Likewise, Lonsdale has seen renewed use of its sportswear by the far right in part because, he says, when worn a certain way the logo spells out NSDA — the abbreviation for Germany's National Socialist Party.
"Those who know will know; those who don't know will think this is harmless," Botsch said.
The ambiguity is significant because Germany's law against Nazi symbols "expressly covers flags, badges, uniform items, slogans and forms of greeting,” said Sophie Scheuble, digital policy and counter-extremism manager at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.
So "most of what is worn at far-right events is therefore lawful, and this distinction is well understood within right-wing extremist scenes.”
Those restrictions have led to an increase in the use of symbols recognizable only to those who know what they mean, without crossing legal lines.
When the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt's domestic intelligence service updated its handbook on far-right symbols in May, Scheuble said, its director noted that most extremists avoid prosecutable symbols and instead rely on codes and catchwords.
What has changed, researchers say, is the political environment where those styles are appearing.
Changing political climate
The Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has grown from a fringe party in 2013 into the likely winner of an upcoming state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The party has been legally designated a far-right extremist group in the state.
If it wins, it would mark the first time a far-right party has had an absolute state majority in Germany since the Second World War.
Fabian Wichmann, an expert at the EU Knowledge Hub on Preventing Radicalization, said there is a growing "grey zone" between Germany's hardcore neo-Nazi movement and the broader populist right.
Members of neo-Nazi groups attend AfD rallies and meetings and have encouraged their supporters to vote for the party, he says, seeing its success as a step toward their own political goals.
"The AfD has a widespread and diverse group of followers," Wichmann said. At its election events and marches, "you will see people who look very normal in their clothing," wearing things like New Balance and Lonsdale.
He said not everyone wearing those brands is a neo-Nazi, but there are "also a lot of neo-Nazis who wear this kind of stuff because they have some typical symbols, some typical narratives they share."
But the bigger change researchers say they're seeing isn't in the clothing itself. It's in the willingness to display those signals openly.

items.title: Days after deadly Nepal flood, families of missing B.C. couples desperate for details
items.body_text:
Days after deadly Nepal flood, families of missing B.C. couples desperate for details
Ottawa says 1 of 32 Canadians unaccounted for in Nepal has been located safely
Days after a massive wall of water tore through the Timure region of Nepal, families of two missing Metro Vancouver couples are desperately searching for information about their loved ones.
Port Moody couple Dhaval and Megha Shah and Coquitlam couple Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla are among thousands of people who are missing after the Aug. 26 flash flood struck, killing at least 676 people.
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of 32 Canadians unaccounted for in the country had been located safely. The person has not been identified.
Vikram Khosla said his cousin Shubakshi was in the area for a trek to Kailash Mansarovar in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others, as a 50th birthday gift to herself.
He said the couple had been almost ready to depart for their journey when they spoke with a family member about an hour before the flood struck on Wednesday morning.
No one has heard from anyone in the group since then, he said.
“We are very hopeful that they went up and they are stuck somewhere," he said.
The couple, Singaporean citizens who moved to Canada about four years ago, have two daughters, he said.
Speaking from Mumbai, India, Dhaval's brother Kheval Shah told CBC his brother and sister-in-law were staying at Hotel Kailash, near the border, on Wednesday.
The family last heard from the two that morning as they were having breakfast, about 15 minutes before the flood struck.
“That hotel is completely submerged, there is no hotel anymore," he said.
“We just want to find out where they were when the water hit.... Ultimately I feel that closure is very important.”
The couple have a 24-year-old daughter, he added.
Canada has said it will send $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal, with the money earmarked for organizations like the Red Cross to deliver assistance to people on the ground.
But Shah said he wants the Canadian government to push Nepal for more information about the search for the missing.
Khosla, too, shared frustration with the lack of updates.
He said Shubakshi's brother and sister have flown to Kathmandu and are trying to get to the affected area to search for answers.
He wants to see a centralized source of information for the families of missing people to get real time updates.
As of Saturday afternoon, more than 3,700 people had been rescued, but another 2,426 people remained missing.
With files from Georgie Smyth, Tanya Fletcher and The Canadian Press
