items.title: Angola Is Emerging as One of Africa’s Most Important Gateways to the Asia-Pacific
items.summary: The story of its success has not been straightforward.
items.body_text:
Angola’s city of Lobito, resting behind a natural harbor on the Western side of Africa, is becoming a major industrial port city. It is the second largest port along Angola’s coast, and it has grown steadily over the course of the last two decades, strategically placed as the head point of the internationally funded Lobito Corridor. The story of its success has not been straightforward. The Benguela Railway runs from Lobito into the heart of Africa, bearing critical minerals like cobalt and copper from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. But Angola’s export wealth has only recently turned towards minerals and, in the past, it focused on oil exports from terminals and offshore reserves at Cabinda and Luanda. Oil markets are volatile, and lower global oil prices in 2014 plunged Angola into a severe economic depression, shaking its energy resource-driven economy and paving the way for the diversified market that is developing across Angola today. It is a market uniquely expanding into global trade, and it will be critical for Asia-Pacific energy supplies and trade links in the long run.
Angola has now paid back the majority of its infrastructural loans to China, bringing the peak of total borrowing from $45 billion in 2000 to roughly $12 billion today. Angola has steadily repaid its debt without restructuring, paying off more than necessary during its payment cycles, and showcasing an ‘Angola Model’ of using oil-backed loans which have become uniquely favorable positions in the midst of recent rises in global oil prices. For development loans where oil revenues do not contribute to repayment, Angola has found unique opportunities to readjust repayment plans for fiscal sustainability. For example, the country announced a “debt-for-education” swap with the World Bank’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency in March of this year. The deal converts debt repayments into investments in education. The savings on interest will be fully applied to an educational program that spans all 21 provinces, aiming to empower girls’ school attendance, human capital, and access to education. The $400 million agreement was finalized in late July, with disbursements to over thirty schools beginning immediately, impacting over 32,000 students.
The debt restructuring is a novel way to continue development even after loans have served their infrastructural purposes, and it represents Angola’s fiscal responsibility, ambitiously aimed at diversifying its own economy. Angola has also stepped up on the world stage. The crisis in the Gulf, which has strangled energy supplies for much of Asia, turned out to become a major opportunity for Angola. For example, President João Lourenço inaugurated a major aluminum plant in Bengo Province in January. That factory now puts out 240 tons of ingots daily, pouring into the 9 percent gap in supplies caused by the closure of Hormuz. Furthermore, Angola’s natural gas reserves are contributing to $2 billion in new investments for an Ammonia-Urea complex, one that, when it opens in 2027, will produce roughly 4,000 tons of fertilizer per day. Angolan trade is not only expanding into novel markets, but traditional markets are also tapping into its supply. Australia, Vietnam, and Hong Kong are likely candidates to increase imports from Angola. The oil sector dominates these new networks; however, they lead to expanded cooperation along the supply chain, especially as Angolan markets build out more value-added industry. These emerging links are particularly significant for the Asia-Pacific, where demand for energy and industrial inputs is reshaping supply chains.
In the case of Vietnam, Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng suggested that cooperation with Angola needed to accelerate, considering Angola’s recent role as Chair of the African Union. items.title: Mongolia Hosts COP17, Urging Global Partners to Action on Climate Issues
items.summary: Mongolia wanted to see “a shift from talk to action” at COP17. The results were mixed.
items.body_text:
The 17th Conference of the Parties to the U.N Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP17) was convened in Ulaanbaatar from August 17-28, bringing together 196 country representatives plus the European Union to negotiate action-based measures on several climate challenges facing the world today. This year’s COP17 included segments on finance, water, land and people, and food systems. Parties agreed on a new initiative that includes $1.3 billion in financing, but failed to approve a new financial mechanism to combat drought.
On August 17, the opening ceremony was attended by Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa, U.N. Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed, Executive Secretary of the UNCCD Dr. Yasmin Fouad, Saudi Arabia’s Deputy Minister of Environment, Water and Agriculture (and president of UNCCD COP16) Dr. Osama Ibrahim Fakiha, and Mongolia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Batmunkh Battsetseg. The global climate gathering also included a visit by South Korea’s former president, Moon Jae-in, and business leaders from Rio Tinto, Trade Development, Oyu Tolgoi, Asian Development Bank, Global Green Growth Institute, and more.
Welcoming the guests and opening the COP17 gathering, Mongolian Prime Minister Uchral Nyam-Osor stated: “The greatest change we want to see from COP17 is a shift from talk to action, from targets to implementation, and from commitments to measurable results.”
As Fouad, the UNCCD executive secretary, put it in an interview with The Diplomat before the gathering: “COP17 comes at a pivotal moment for global action on land… I believe countries will come to Mongolia with a shared understanding that the challenge is no longer understanding the problem – we know what is at stake. The priority now is implementation.”
In the last two weeks, the Mongolian government, civil society, and environmental organizations cooperated with global financial institutions, policymakers, businesses, and environmental scientists to advance solutions to emerging issues facing not just Mongolia but the globe, including desertification, drought, and land degradation. Building on the progress made at COP16 in Riyadh, governments at COP17 aimed to negotiate practical tools, partnerships, and financing mechanisms needed to help countries turn existing plans into action.
According to the UNCCD, more than 70 countries have now developed national drought plans, compared with only three in 2013 – reflecting growing recognition that drought must be managed proactively rather than only once it becomes a humanitarian and economic crisis.
Desertification, land degradation, and climate change are all interconnected and demand integrated solutions. In Mongolia, the challenge includes extreme climate fluctuations, such as dzud and drought, as well as loss of water, water pollution due to mining activities, as well as mismanagement of rangelands and pastoralism. The combination of these issues in turn becomes additional hindrance to the country’s development.
The last two days of COP17 were designated for all 197 parties to come to some sort of an agreement on a mechanism to combat drought. The Asian Development Bank Partnership estimated $355 billion is needed every year to combat land degradation and drought, yet current investment stands at only around $77 billion, leaving an annual financing gap of $278 billion.
Unfortunately, on August 28, last day of the COP17, parties failed to come to an agreement and passed the issue to the next COP gathering.
One of the main disagreements was whether to establish a new drought protocol initiated by the African Group. The bloc of developed countries – including the European Union, Australia, and the United Kingdom – opposed the establishment of a new drought protocol, preferring to utilize previously agreed multilateral frameworks such as Global Environment Facility and to avoid overlapping agreements.

items.title: Tim Cook’s Dark Legacy in China
items.summary: Cook’s leadership perfected Apple’s production – but Chinese workers paid the price.
items.body_text:
On September 1, 2026, Tim Cook will hand over control of Apple to John Ternus. He leaves behind one of the most efficient manufacturing systems in consumer electronics, one he helped build as operations chief from 1998.
In China, Cook leaves a second, but related, legacy: workers on Apple lines toiling 60 hours a week or more, often without a rest day and depending on overtime to cover the basic cost of living.
Ternus will have to decide how to handle both of these realities.
At China Labor Watch, we just completed a new investigation into Apple’s supply chains in China. Our conclusion is not simply that Apple’s compliance system fails to prevent violations. Many of the labor conditions that the report identified are baked into the production model itself.
I once asked a worker on an Apple line at a Foxconn factory what he made of the human rights standards Western countries talk about. He called them Western propaganda. What taught him about America, he said, was not standards on paper but the machine-like pace of Apple’s line and pay he was never sure would arrive.
Since 2006 we have investigated Apple’s suppliers in China, publishing 19 reports. I have come to believe blaming Apple alone would be unfair. Apple’s supply chain in China was built on a trade. China needed foreign capital, technology, and jobs. In return, Western firms got cheap labor and speed built on long overtime and extreme scheduling flexibility.
The Chinese government, Apple, and the supplier factories all bear responsibility for the conditions workers face. But Apple has treated allegations of wrongdoing as a compliance problem, rather than the output of its own production model.
Apple’s product cycles are fast, and launches send order volumes sharply higher. Suppliers work on thin margins and must deliver enormous volumes quickly. The component prices are set; equipment costs are sunk. There is only one place left to ensure profits: labor costs. Workers’ hours and income become the buffer, absorbing the volatility Apple itself generates.
Apple’s answer has been to police this through a Supplier Code of Conduct, audits, public reporting and worker training. While these steps do have an impact, the overall pattern is clear: individual violations may be corrected, but the same problems return.
In 2019 we found withheld wages at Foxconn’s Zhengzhou plant. At the same plant, more than half the workforce was on dispatch contracts, far above the legal cap of 10 percent. Apple disputed most of our findings but acknowledged excessive use of dispatch workers. In 2022 thousands at the same plant clashed with police over pay promised at recruitment; Foxconn apologized, blaming a computer input error. In 2025 we found dispatch workers still being used above the legal cap.
This August we found a full-time assembly worker at Foxconn’s Zhengzhou plant on a base wage of 2,450 yuan a month, about $363, a little above the city’s legal minimum of 2,350 yuan. To reach 4,200 yuan he has to work 60-hour weeks, totaling roughly 87 hours of overtime a month, against a statutory ceiling of 36.
Raising his base wage by 1,750 yuan, about $260 a month, would let him earn the income he needs on a legal schedule. Even if all 200,000 workers employed at peak operating times received that increase for a full year, the cost would be roughly $620 million – about half of one percent of Apple’s $112 billion in net income in the year to September.
Clearly, Apple can afford to pay more. The discrepancy, then, points to a deeper issue: labor conditions are not given the same priority as output, speed, and profit margin.
Look at how Apple manages suppliers. Yield rates and delivery deadlines are tracked precisely. Missing them can cost a supplier its orders. A labor violation, by contrast, will just produce another audit. Foxconn went through the 2010 suicides and has gone through one labor dispute after another since. To this day it remains one of Apple’s most important partners.

items.title: In defense of Asian American art
items.summary: Back in 2015, when I was living in Brooklyn, my apartment flooded. My landlord, who owned a bunch of apartments, offered to put me up in temporary accommodations. He and his girlfriend were going to be out of town for several months, so he let me stay in her room. items.body_text:
Back in 2015, when I was living in Brooklyn, my apartment flooded. My landlord, who owned a bunch of apartments, offered to put me up in temporary accommodations. He and his girlfriend were going to be out of town for several months, so he let me stay in her room.
His girlfriend was an aspiring actress from Minnesota named Poppy Liu. I got to interact with her a number of times, and I can say that she’s one of the more interesting and original people I’ve ever met.
Poppy finally made it big. One of her latest roles is as the voice actress for one of the protagonists on the new animated Netflix series DANG!, a story about three Asian Americans living in NYC:
The show isn’t out yet, but from what I can tell, DANG! is trying to tell a story that will resonate with second-generation Asian Americans[1] — one of the characters is a striver who goes off the beaten path, the others were escaping their striver upbringing by leading nontraditional lifestyles from the get-go. That’s probably a pretty typical real-world experience for the American-born children of high-skilled immigrants.
I don’t know if the show will be good or not, but as soon as the trailer hit, people on Twitter started ridiculing it — and using it as an opportunity to make fun of “Asian American media” or “Asian American art” in general. Some of the comments were dour and downbeat:
…While other commentary was pretty hilarious:
It turns out that Asian Americans bashing “Asian American art” is a pretty well-established tradition. Here’s another example unrelated to the Netflix show:
(See also here.)
It’s always fun to rag on tired tropes. But I feel like I should stand up for Asian American art here, because there really is a lot of excellent stuff out there that doesn’t fit into the standard format that people are complaining about.
“Asian American art” is defined too narrowly
The biggest problem with “Asian American art”, as far as I can tell, is that it’s defined so narrowly that there really isn’t much room for it to be creative. Consider these two possible definitions of “Asian American art”:
- Art made by Asian Americans
- Art made about Asian Americans or Asian American culture
As far as I can tell, movies, TV shows, books, etc. only get labeled “Asian American” if they satisfy both of these criteria at once. But that’s a pretty narrow slice of art!
First, it excludes art made about Asian Americans by non-Asians. There isn’t really a lot of this around, because America’s modern approach to identity politics says that you should only write about a group of people if you’re from that group — if a white author writes a novel with an Asian American protagonist, it’s generally frowned upon.
There are some notable exceptions that get grandfathered in — Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle was written and directed by three white guys — but the culture of the 2010s really put a damper on that sort of crossover.
That means a lot of interesting and insightful stories about Asian Americans probably never get told. For example, I thought Ernest Hemingway’s portrayal of a frustrated Jewish striver in The Sun Also Rises was incredibly deep and thoughtful, and managed to say lots of things about how second-generation Jewish Americans were integrating into American society at the time.
That portrayal probably wouldn’t get written today — a lot of people now accuse it of being antisemitic,[2] because the character, while complex and sympathetic, is deeply flawed, and Hemingway himself wasn’t Jewish.
It also means that works clearly inspired by Asian America don’t generally get recognized as such. The clearest example of this is Avatar: the Last Airbender, which was arguably the best new fantasy IP to come out of the US since the turn of the century.[3] ATLA, as it’s sometimes known, drew on a bunch of Asian cultures — mostly Chinese, but also Japanese, Tibetan, Korean, and others — to create a sort of pan-Asian mishmash, informed by American sensibilities and written in a distinctl

items.title: Bangladesh’s J-10CE fighter plan stirs China dependence fears
items.summary: Bangladesh’s planned J-10CE purchase could significantly strengthen its airpower while tying that capability more closely to Chinese weapons, support networks and supply chains. This month, multiple media outlets reported that Bangladesh is moving toward one of its largest defense procurements in years, preparing to buy Chinese J-10CE fighter jets as part of an air force […] The post Bangladesh’s J-10CE fighter plan stirs China dependence fears appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
Bangladesh’s planned J-10CE purchase could significantly strengthen its airpower while tying that capability more closely to Chinese weapons, support networks and supply chains.
This month, multiple media outlets reported that Bangladesh is moving toward one of its largest defense procurements in years, preparing to buy Chinese J-10CE fighter jets as part of an air force modernization drive that would deepen its ties with China, its biggest arms supplier.
A draft proposal has been sent to Bangladesh’s Finance Ministry and Armed Forces Division for final approval, with the package also covering attack helicopters, VIP transport helicopters and unmanned aerial systems; procurement could begin in the current fiscal year if funding is allocated or roll into the next budget cycle.
Bangladesh is considering 20 to 24 aircraft, with the cost rising from a base of US$62.7 million per jet to nearly $115 million once training, logistics, infrastructure and related expenses are included.
The J-10CE’s reported performance may have influenced Bangladesh’s choice in the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict, when Pakistan said the aircraft helped shoot down Indian fighters, including Rafales, claims that remain disputed. Pakistan is the sole confirmed foreign operator of the export type.
Bangladesh’s prospective J-10CE acquisition would therefore do more than modernize its fighter fleet: realizing the aircraft’s full potential could pull the country deeper into China’s combat ecosystem, narrowing its tactical gap with India while increasing long-term operational dependence on Chinese support.
Previously, Asia Times reported that Bangladesh is planning to acquire China-Pakistan JF-17 Thunder Block III fighters to modernize its aging fleet of F-7s and MiG-29s, equipping them with beyond-visual-range missiles and advanced avionics.
The J-10 and JF-17 would occupy complementary roles. The heavier J-10 emphasizes air superiority, advanced radar and greater aerodynamic performance, while the lighter JF-17 offers a cheaper, easier-to-maintain multirole platform.
Together, they could give Bangladesh a high-low fighter mix, with J-10s assigned to more demanding air-superiority missions and JF-17s handling routine combat air patrol and strike duties.
Chinese fighters are a logical modernization option given their comparatively low cost, Bangladesh’s decades of experience operating Chinese equipment and established procurement ties with China.
Pakistan’s reported J-10CE performance against India in May 2025 may have depended as much on the wider combat network supporting the fighters as on the aircraft themselves. Pakistan operated the jets within a broader Chinese-origin ecosystem, meaning acquiring the J-10CE alone may not reproduce the capabilities demonstrated during the clashes.
During the clashes, Pakistan’s Chinese-made ground-based air defenses reportedly targeted Indian aircraft, while Pakistan’s China-made fighters launched missiles guided by a Chinese-origin airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft.
Dependence on that ecosystem also exposes buyers to platform reliability and supply-chain risks. For instance, JF-17 fighters supplied to Myanmar have reportedly suffered structural and technical issues, with the airframes vulnerable to damage during high-G maneuvers.
Additional alleged defects include maintenance and accuracy issues with the JF-17’s KLJ-7 Al radar and malfunctions in the aircraft’s weapon mission management computer, which hinder the type’s beyond-visual-range combat capability.
The JF-17s in Myanmar’s service also suffer from a lack of spare parts because Western sanctions on Myanmar have prevented Myanmar from obtaining the Western avionics and electronics installed in the type.
Over the past 20 years, China has provided Bangladesh with ships, fighter aircraft, tanks, and missile systems, accounting for 70% of the country’s arms purchases. But the strategic significance of those sales extends beyond the weapons themselve

items.title: Holy See seeks a path to peace in Moscow
items.summary: While Bishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s Secretary for Relations with States, was holding a press conference with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, another Catholic official landed in Moscow: CIA Director John Ratcliffe – who reportedly went to Moscow to warn Russia against support for Iran and activities in Europe. Vatican diplomacy and American […] The post Holy See seeks a path to peace in Moscow appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
While Bishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s Secretary for Relations with States, was holding a press conference with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, another Catholic official landed in Moscow: CIA Director John Ratcliffe – who reportedly went to Moscow to warn Russia against support for Iran and activities in Europe.
Vatican diplomacy and American intelligence crossed paths in an effort to restore some balance to a chaotic world order and establish dialogue as a basis for viable peace.
On Tuesday, August 25, long-term diplomatic planning and last-minute intelligence briefings came together in the Russian capital. Moscow became the meeting place where the Vatican’s diplomatic efforts to promote peace and American global interests in foreign affairs converged.
Russian television transmitted the beginning and end of the meeting between Bishop Gallagher and Minister Lavrov live. The introductory statements at the negotiating table and the final remarks at the press conference were carefully prepared in advance and presumably agreed upon.
Both sides wanted more than just media coverage of the meeting; they wanted to demonstrate that, despite its difficulties, dialogue is still possible. Bishop Gallagher, on behalf of Pope Leo and Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin, presented the international community with the challenging reality that wars cannot be ended militarily today.
Diplomacy is needed, and it should also be the means by which conflicts are resolved before they reach the point of military intervention or, worse, war.
Bishop Gallagher said that those involved in the conflict, along with the entire international community, must establish conditions conducive to “serious political and diplomatic work.” The Holy See is prepared to offer diplomatic and ecclesial support to achieve peace in Ukraine.
Lavrov stressed the balance of Vatican diplomacy regarding the situation in Ukraine, acknowledging the Holy See’s initiatives to settle the conflict. Lavrov announced that Moscow is ready to resume political consultations at the deputy foreign minister level regarding this conflict and praised the Holy See’s diplomatic efforts and its “active involvement in resolving a number of acute humanitarian issues in the Ukrainian conflict.”
Another issue discussed in the meeting was the AI, particularly its use in the military. Ascertaining aligned positions on such topic, the Holy See and the Russian Federation agreed to carry on the dialogue in a substantive way.
As expected, Lavrov brought up the issue of the Russian-speaking population in Ukraine and the Ukrainian government’s actions against the Ukrainian Orthodox Church in communion with the Moscow Patriarchate, led by Kirill. Lavrov used precise canonical and theological terminology in the latter case.
Bishop Anthony of Volokolamsk, chairman of the Department for External Church Relations of the Moscow Patriarchate, also addressed the question about “the persecution of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church by the Ukrainian state authorities” during his meeting with Bishop Gallagher.
Although potentially divisive, this issue does not seem significant enough to impede positive developments in Vatican-Russian diplomatic relations, as both Lavrov and Gallagher stated that they expect to achieve progress and further cooperation with their counterparts.
While the Gallagher-Lavrov meeting received widespread public attention, the meeting between Bishop Gallagher and Yuri Ushakov, Putin’s advisor for international affairs, was held discreetly and confidentially, as is customary when counterparts wish to take decisive steps forward in their diplomatic relations.
The Holy See announced the meeting’s occurrence with a post on the X account of the State Secretariat.

The US has a secret plan for Libya. It will backfire
For nearly a year, Massad Boulos, US President Donald Trump’s senior advisor on Arab, Middle Eastern, and African Affairs, has aggressively pursued a diplomatic circuit connecting Tripoli, Benghazi, Paris, Rome, and Abu Dhabi. His primary objective is to push a transactional political settlement designed to resolve Libya’s administrative paralysis and the internal west-east divide by formalizing an alliance between the country’s rival power centers.
Taking shape behind closed doors since last September, first in Rome then across other capitals, the core mechanism of this US-brokered blueprint is a restructuring of the executive presidency: placing Saddam Haftar (Commander of Ground Forces in eastern Libya and deputy to his father) at the helm of a reformed Presidential Council, while keeping Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh as Prime Minister. Rather than fostering a democratic transition, the framework accepts state fragmentation as a permanent reality, securing the Dbeibeh administration in the west and the Haftar family network in the east as a dynastic duopoly.
To pave the way for such initiatives, Washington has leveraged preliminary milestones. In April, Boulos helped broker a record 190 billion dinar unified budget agreement – the first in Libya since 2014. At the same time, joint military maneuvers were executed in Sirte under AFRICOM’s Flintlock exercises, bringing together east and west forces alongside participation from Italy and over a dozen African nations.
Treating this unwritten transactional design as a national settlement fundamentally misreads the crisis.
Rather than establishing a legally grounded framework for general elections or dismantling entrenched militia networks, the arrangement codifies an elite duopoly. By relying on temporary financial distributions and supervised unified military drills to broker a top-down truce, Washington is mistaking a fragile pact between ruling families for actual state-building – guaranteeing that Libya’s hydrocarbon wealth continues to line the pockets of an entrenched cartel at the expense of its people.
Crucially, the Boulos initiative operates as an unwritten diplomatic push devoid of statutory grounding. By ignoring the foundational UN Security Council resolutions that grant legal mandate to external mediation, Washington’s ad-hoc gamble lacks the institutional backing required to bind local actors. Furthermore, the plan offers no long-term enforcement mechanisms. It relies on current US political backing and provides no protocol if the newly installed executives simply refuse to vacate power after the proposed two-to-three-year interim.
Without a universally accepted arbiter to compel compliance, the initiative risks becoming a dangerous power trap, leaving Libya vulnerable to renewed confrontation the moment external priorities shift.
This bilateral push also directly collides with the ongoing UN-led mediation process overseen by the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL). While the UN’s incremental track has certainly been slow and struggled to deliver a breakthrough, it remains anchored in UNSC mandates and operates through recognized, albeit heavily discredited, domestic institutions – such as the House of Representatives and the High Council of State. By attempting to bypass these constitutional bodies in favor of an elite shortcut, Washington risks completely undermining the delicate institutional consensus UNSMIL has spent years attempting to build. Replacing a broad-based, rules-driven process with a fast-tracked bargain creates a parallel route that further fragments international diplomatic efforts and deepens institutional paralysis.

items.summary: South Africa has recorded 3,462 measles cases since January, health officials have said Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
South Africa records over 3,400 measles cases
South Africa has recorded 3,462 confirmed measles cases since January 2026, with outbreaks reported in the Western Cape, Free State, KwaZulu-Natal, and Northern Cape, among children aged one to 14 years, the country’s Department of Health said on Wednesday.
Department spokesperson Foster Mohale said the proportion of unvaccinated children under one year old had increased from 12.1% in 2017 to an alarming 36.3% between January and April 2026. This effectively triples the number of completely unvaccinated children and leaves hundreds of thousands of infants at risk of life-threatening illnesses.
Mohale added routine immunisation coverage had fallen severely across all 52 districts in the country, which means that, at current rates, South Africa is unlikely to reach the World Health Organization’s critical 90% coverage threshold for childhood immunisation. He said the consequences of declining coverage include the resurgence of serious vaccine-preventable diseases, erosion of community, or herd immunity, and higher rates of long-term disability and death among infants.
“The majority of cases (70.9%) are in children aged 1–14 years, directly linked to low immunisation coverage,” Mohale stressed.
Mohale added that South Africa has maintained its polio-free status since 2014, while sporadic cases of diphtheria had been detected, primarily in the Western Cape, underscoring gaps in booster coverage and disease surveillance. Pertussis, or whooping cough, cases have also been identified in several provinces, predominantly affecting infants under six months who are too young to be fully vaccinated, Mohale said.
According to spokesperson, this poses severe risks for pregnant women because of the potential for congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). “Unvaccinated children can endanger infants and immunocompromised individuals who cannot be vaccinated, and weak coverage undermines early detection and rapid response to emerging threats.”
Mohale said the department is prioritising an immediate, coordinated national response, including catch-up vaccination campaigns targeting children who have missed doses and under-immunised cohorts in all districts. “Every child deserves protection, and safeguarding them is a collective responsibility,” he concluded.

items.title: Zambian opposition leader detained
items.summary: Zambia’s opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate have been detained as police investigate alleged treason Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Zambian opposition leader detained
Zambia’s main opposition leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu have been accused of treason and detained after being questioned, the Zambia Police Service said on Thursday.
Mundubile and Zulu were questioned “in connection with an alleged offence of treason,” police said. Officers did not provide specifics about the nature of the transgression. The two remain in custody at Lusaka Central Police while investigations continue, according to local outlets.
The detention comes two weeks after Zambia’s presidential election, in which Mundubile finished second to Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema. Official results gave Hichilema about 60% of the vote and Mundubile about 38%. Mundubile rejected the result and said he intended to challenge it in court over alleged irregularities, claims Hichilema has denied.
Tensions rose after the vote when security forces raided Mundubile’s residence in Lusaka. Eleven people, including those associated with the opposition, were detained during the operation, where former transport and communications minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was fatally shot, according to police.
Police Chief Graphel Musamba said the task force encountered “gunfire and resistance from unknown individuals” and returned fire. The government said military-grade weapons, ammunition and other materials intended for use in an armed insurrection were found at the property.
Mundubile rejected the accusations as “total fabrications” and described the raid as an attempt on his life. Following the operation, he and Zulu, citing concerns for their safety, took shelter at the UN offices on Alick Nkhata Road in Lusaka, the local outlet Lusaka Times said. They stayed at the compound until Thursday, when they surrendered to police after receiving assurances from the presidency that they would be afforded due process.
Under Zambia’s Penal Code, treason carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. The country abolished the death penalty in 2022.
Hichilema, who first took office in 2021, is due to begin a second five-year term following the latest vote.

items.summary: Following the recitation of the midday Angelus prayer from Castel Gandolfo on Sunday, Pope Leo XIV condemned the recent massacre in Haiti, made an urgent appeal for the release of hostages, and renewed his call for concrete assistance to Nepal following devastating floods and mudslides that have killed hundreds and left thousands missing. items.body_text:
Pope Leo urges release of Haiti hostages, aid for Nepal after deadly floods
By Deborah Castellano Lubov
âFrom Haiti come terrible reports of the grave massacre perpetrated in Kenscoff, in which numerous people have lost their lives while others have been kidnapped. I express my prayerful closeness to the victims and their families and ask that all the hostages be released without delay. I make a heartfelt appeal to all those responsible to make a concrete commitment to ensuring the safety of the population and putting an end to every form of violence.â
Pope Leo XIV made the appeal following the recitation of the Angelus prayer on Sunday at noon in Castel Gandolfo, where he stayed overnight after taking part Saturday evening in the Marian procession of Our Lady of the Lake on Lake Albano.
Alleviate the suffering of Nepal and Tibet
Following the appeal for Haiti, Pope Leo assured those affected by the devastating flooding in Nepal and Tibet of his prayers. He invited the faithful to pray for those who have died, the injured and missing, their families, and the rescuers involved in the ongoing emergency response.
âMay everyoneâs concern and commitment," he prayed, "help to alleviate suffering and bring the necessary assistance to the affected populations.â
The Vatican announced Saturday that Pope Leo, through the Dicastery for the Service of Charity, had sent financial assistance to Caritas Nepal to help meet the most urgent needs of people affected by the disaster.
Death toll exceeds 700 and thousands displaced
In coordination with the Apostolic Nunciature of Nepal, the Popeâs contribution will support Caritas Nepal, which operates under the direction of the Apostolic Vicariate, in its relief efforts. These began in the first hours following the disaster and include providing food, basic necessities, and shelter to people who have lost everything.
Relief operations are continuing as the death toll in the affected regions rises, with more than 700 people reported dead between Nepal and Tibet and at least 3,000 still missing.
In a telegram sent Thursday and signed by Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin, Pope Leo expressed his sorrow over the loss of life and widespread destruction. He commended the souls of those who died âto the clemency of the Almightyâ and offered his heartfelt condolences to the bereaved.
He also assured those affected by the disaster of his spiritual closeness and prayed for the emergency personnel engaged in ongoing search-and-rescue operations.
A renewed appeal for peace
Pope Leo then urged the faithful to continue praying for peace, recalling the words of Saint Augustine, whose liturgical memorial was celebrated on August 28.
The Pope recalled Augustineâs image of peace as being like âthe bread of the miracle that grew in the hands of the disciples as they broke it and distributed it.â
âMay the number increase throughout the world,â he prayed, âof those who courageously break and distribute the bread of peace, overcoming divisions, promoting justice, and practicing forgiveness, for the good of all.â
Prayer for Creation
Finally, the Holy Father recalled in English that on Tuesday, September 1, the Church will celebrate the World Day of Prayer for the Care of Creation.
âThis marks the beginning of the Season of Creation â observed by Christians of various denominations â whose theme this year is âLiving Water.ââ
âAs I recalled in the Message for this Day,â Pope Leo reiterated, âcaring for our common home calls for a conversion of heart, so that what has been used to bring about destruction may instead be directed toward life.â
âI invite everyone to join in prayer and action, that we may become channels of the living water of Godâs peace, refreshing our wounded world.â

items.title: Pope at Angelus: Even when confused like Peter, dialogue with the Lord
items.summary: During his Sunday Angelus address in Castel Gandolfo, Pope Leo XIV reminds the faithful that St. Peter was very human and that, like him, we ought to “humbly tell Jesus what we truly feel, even when our hearts are confused." Read all
items.body_text:
Pope at Angelus: Even when confused like Peter, dialogue with the Lord
By Deborah Castellano Lubov
âIn our life of faith and in our prayer, may we have the same sincerity as Peter, humbly telling Jesus what we truly feel, even when our hearts are confused.â
Pope Leo XIV gave this advice during his Angelus address on Sunday in Castel Gandolfo, where he stayed overnight after joining in the Marian procession of Our Lady of the Lake on Lake Albano the previous evening.
In his catechesis, the Holy Father recalled the dayâs Gospel reading according to Saint Matthew, in which Jesus reveals to His disciples the mystery of His impending Passion, Death and Resurrection.
Human nature
The Pope acknowledged that what the Lord says is a far cry from our expectations of a triumphant and powerful Messiah, with whose help they would defeat their enemies, and how Peter expressed his disagreement and, surprised and disappointed, rebuked Jesus, saying to Him: ââGod forbid it, Lord! This must never happen to you.ââ
The Pope suggested that this makes us think about our human nature.
âFor us, too,â he acknowledged, âit is not always easy to understand and accept Godâs ways, especially when they are very far from our own.â
He also recognized that âthe temptation arises, against all the reasoning of faith, to think that the Lord is the one who is wrong,â or âworse still, that He is not listening to us or is not concerned about us.â
St. Peter teaches us important lessons
Faced with this uncertainty, Pope Leo underscored that Peter, even in his impulsiveness, teaches us two important things.
âThe first is, even in such moments,â he said, ânever to cease our dialogue with the Lord.â
Instead, he proposed, âwe are confidently to tell Him our difficulty in understanding what He is asking of us.â
The second, he continued, âis never to judge Godâs work, but rather humbly and prayerfully to listen to what He is revealing to us through His actions, even when they do not meet our expectations.â
Pope Leo noted that the greatness of the first of the Apostles is also evident in this.
Pope Leo recalled that Jesus replies, âGet behind me, Satan!â and explains to him and the other disciples that, to follow in His footsteps, they must deny themselves, take up their crosses, and follow Him, pointing out to the faithful that âPeter will do just that.â
âAfter listening to Him, Peter," the Pope said, "will accept the challenge and remain faithful to the words of Christ, whom he has recognized as his Redeemer, for the rest of his life, even unto martyrdom.â
Blessed Motherâs obedience to her Son even at foot of Cross
Thus, the Holy Father invited the faithful to join him in asking the Lord âthat we, too, in our life of faith and in our prayer, may have the same sincerity as Peter, humbly telling Jesus what we truly feel, even when our hearts are confused.â
âAt the same time,â he continued, âmay we cultivate Peterâs own docility in accepting what Jesus asks of us beyond our expectations.â
Pope Leo concluded by praying that the Blessed Virgin Mary, who âwas obedient to Godâs plans even at the foot of the cross of her Son Jesus,â help us with her example.

items.title: Archbishop Gallagher: The Holy See pursues a diplomacy that believes in peace
items.summary: At the end of his mission to Moscow, the Holy See's Secretary for Relations with States and International Organizations, Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, speaks to Vatican News about his journey. Read all
items.body_text:
Archbishop Gallagher: The Holy See pursues a diplomacy that believes in peace
By Stefano Leszczynski
The sun was shining in Moscow on Friday in the early afternoon when the head of the Holy Seeâs diplomacy boarded the flight that took him back to Rome, via Istanbul, to return to the Vatican late at night. It was a long and rather cumbersome journey. The suspension of direct connections between Russia and the countries of the European Union, in fact, restricts the options for reaching Moscow and obliges the few scheduled flights to make a long detour around Europe, which from Istanbul leads to crossing the Balkans, skirting the Ukrainian borders and, finally, crossing the skies of Belarus. It took at least twelve hours, between flights and stopovers, for a journey that before 2022 required about four hours of flying.
âIt was a long journey,â confirms Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, âbut this too takes on a symbolic dimension â before 2022, one reached Moscow in a few hours, whereas today the road has become longer. This journey is indicative of the desire for the dialogue that the Holy See wants to pursue. A dialogue that we have been conducting for years, both through the Embassy of the Russian Federation to the Holy See and through the work of the Apostolic Nuncio Archbishop Giovanni dâAniello in Moscow. This underscores the commitment and the importance that we have attributed to this journey, which was undertaken on behalf of the Holy See and with the blessing of the Pope.â
Q: There was evident appreciation on the part of the Russian authorities for your trip to Moscow, which emerged from the institutional talks with Foreign Minister Lavrov and Adviser Ushakov. The issue of the ongoing war with Ukraine captured much of the attention. You have stressed several times that the only way to end the hostilities is a return to diplomacy.
Yes, it is a difficult dialogue, because the longer the war continues, the more difficult it will be to restore relations: there are many victims, many open wounds. But we know very well that, historically, all conflicts, all wars end with a negotiation, with an agreement, and then one begins to restore relations between the former belligerents. In this sense, diplomacy offers and promises a possible solution. This is also what we, as a Church, have the responsibility and the duty to proclaim. We went to Moscow to speak of peace, to encourage souls troubled by war, and to say: have courage, embrace the path of peace, have the hope of believing in a better day. And I believe that essentially this was our message.
Q: After the bilateral meeting, Foreign Minister Lavrov said in an interview that during the talks, you limited yourself rather to a general appeal to put an end to the conflict as soon as possible.
Yes, it is true, this is precisely our line, which we have always maintained. The Holy See does not enter into the details of the negotiations, nor does it propose technical solutions, because this is the direct responsibility of the belligerent parties. The Holy See, instead, recalls this responsibility and invites them to show goodwill in order to seriously begin a dialogue. And it does so by addressing both the Russian Federation and Ukraine, as well as other countries, asking that no effort be spared to create spaces for dialogue.
Q: In the face of the suffering of civilian populations because of the war, you have maintained the need to strengthen humanitarian action, given also the trip that Cardinal Matteo Zuppi will make to the Russian Federation. What are the priorities?
This dimension is fundamental and, in this area, the Holy See is already offering its contribution, a commitment that so far has been greatly appreciated. The Holy Father himself, before I left, told me: we must insist on the humanitarian dimension. And that is what we did.
We hope that Cardinal Zuppiâs peace mission will continue and that he will be able to return promptly to Moscow, also in order to be a witness to
